A pre-trained model is one that a provider has already built and trained on very large amounts of data, so you do not have to train your own. An API (application programming interface) is a defined way for your program to send a request to a service and receive a result. Google Cloud's pre-trained APIs package such models behind requests you can make from code. The Vision API reads images and returns things such as labels, detected objects, and text found inside a picture. The Translation API converts text from one language to another. The Speech-to-Text API turns recorded audio into written text. Gemini is a general-purpose generative model: it accepts text and other inputs such as images or audio, and produces new text, for example a summary, a draft, or an answer to a question.

Why this works: each specialised service does one narrow job, so it is usually accurate and predictable at that job. Gemini is broad and can do many tasks, but its output is less constrained, so it is harder to test against a fixed standard.

Worked example: the call-centre company has recorded calls in German and wants an English summary for managers. Step 1: Speech-to-Text turns each audio file into German text. Step 2: Translation turns that German text into English. Step 3: Gemini reads the English transcript and writes a three-sentence summary. Each step has a clear input and a clear output, so you can check each one.

Common mistake: reaching for Gemini first because it sounds the most capable. If the job is only converting audio to text, a speech service is simpler to test, cheaper to run, and its errors are easier to measure.

Consequence: data quality shapes every step. Noisy audio gives a poor transcript, a poor transcript gives a poor translation, and the final summary can still read confidently while being wrong. Measure accuracy on a sample of real recordings before you rely on the chain.

questions.prompt: A parts warehouse photographs supplier labels printed in Korean on incoming pallets, and the team wants the label text in English inside its inventory system. Step 1: the Vision API reads the printed Korean text from each photo and returns it as text. Step 2 is missing: it must convert that Korean text into English text. Step 3: the English text is saved to the inventory record next to the pallet ID. Which Google Cloud product fills the missing step 2?
choices: Gemini, because it is the most capable model and can do any task
The Speech-to-Text API, which turns recorded audio into written text
The Translation API, which converts text from one language to another
The Vision API run a second time on the English text
questions.why: The Translation API is the pre-trained service that converts text between languages, and the Vision API has already produced the text, so the missing step needs a translation service.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a pre-trained API as the teaching text explains it?
choices: A defined way for your program to send a request to a provider's already-trained model and receive a result
A storage bucket where you upload raw training data for later use
A general-purpose text model that writes new content and nothing else
A model you must train from scratch on your own company data before any request will work
questions.why: The teaching text defines an API as a defined way for a program to send a request and receive a result, and a pre-trained model is one the provider has already built and trained.

questions.prompt: A clinic records doctors dictating short voice notes after each visit and wants the notes stored as searchable written text in the patient record. Which Google Cloud product most directly fits this use case?
choices: The Vision API, because it reads text found inside pictures
Gemini, because it accepts audio and produces new text
The Speech-to-Text API, because it turns recorded audio into written text
The Translation API, because it converts text between languages
questions.why: The job is only converting recorded audio into written text, which is the narrow task of the Speech-to-Text API, and the teaching text says a specialised service is simpler to test for that.

questions.prompt: A team chains three services for a monthly report: Speech-to-Text transcribes call recordings, Translation converts them to English, and Gemini writes a summary. The summary reads smoothly, so the manager proposes relying on it at once. What should the team do first, based on the teaching text?
choices: Replace Gemini with a second Gemini call to check the first one's wording
Drop Translation, since English transcripts never need checking
Trust the summary, because a fluent answer from Gemini shows the chain is accurate
Measure accuracy on a sample of real recordings, because noisy audio can produce a poor transcript and a confident but wrong summary
questions.why: The teaching text warns that poor audio leads to poor transcripts and translations, that the final summary can still read confidently while being wrong, and that accuracy should be measured on real recordings before relying on the chain.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between the Vision API, Speech-to-Text, Translation, and Gemini for a new feature, and name one limit or tradeoff of using a pre-trained service instead of building your own model.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by describing the input and the output. If the input is an image and the output is labels or text found in it, the Vision API fits. If the input is audio and the output is a transcript, Speech-to-Text fits. If the text needs to change language, Translation fits. If the output is open-ended, such as a summary, a draft, or an answer that combines several inputs, Gemini fits. I prefer the most specialised service that does the job, because its behaviour is easier to test. The main tradeoff of a pre-trained service is that we cannot change what it was trained on. If our customers use unusual vocabulary, such as internal product codes, accuracy may drop, and we would need to measure that on our own samples before trusting the output.
rubricPoints: Matches each service to its input and output type
Prefers the narrowest service that does the job, for testability and cost
Explains that Gemini is general-purpose and harder to constrain
Names a real limit of pre-trained services, such as fixed training data or unusual vocabulary
Notes that output quality depends on input data quality

suggested.rationale: Choosing between these services is best learned by reasoning through realistic mixed-input business scenarios, which a reasoning exercise covers better than a single existing mission.

lessons.plain: Sometimes a general-purpose AI tool does not know your business well enough. Building a custom model means teaching a program to make predictions or decisions using examples from your own records, such as past support tickets labelled by urgency or invoices labelled as fraudulent or fine. Google Cloud offers managed tools that handle much of the heavy lifting, so a team does not have to write the learning code from scratch. The key idea is that a model is only as good as the examples it learns from, so the quality of your own data matters as much as the tool you pick.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retailer wants to flag which incoming customer emails are complaints about late deliveries. It has ten years of old emails, but staff never recorded which ones were about deliveries. What is the biggest risk to building a useful model from those emails, and why?
lessons.teach: A custom model is a predictive model trained on your organization's own records, rather than one trained in advance on general data. Training data is the set of past examples the model learns from. A label is the correct answer attached to each example, such as urgent or routine on a support ticket. Learning from labelled examples is called supervised learning. AutoML, short for automated machine learning, is a managed approach where the platform tries many model settings and keeps the best performer, so the team does not hand-tune every step. Agent Studio, on the Agent Platform, is a lower-code environment for building AI agents and adapting models to your own content. Why it works: the model finds patterns that link inputs to labels, then applies those patterns to new cases. Worked example: a support team has 20,000 past tickets, each labelled urgent or routine based on how it was eventually handled. Step one, remove duplicates and fix blank fields. Step two, split the data, using about 80 percent for training and holding back 20 percent. Step three, the tool trains and tries settings. Step four, score the model on the held-back tickets it never saw and measure accuracy. Step five, deploy it and keep tracking accuracy over time. Common mistake: testing on tickets the model already trained on, which makes accuracy look far better than it is. Consequence: if labels were recorded inconsistently, the model learns that inconsistency and may send real emergencies to the routine queue with full confidence. Data quality dimensions to check include completeness, uniqueness, timeliness, validity, accuracy and consistency. A model is only as reliable as the data it learns from.

questions.prompt: A hotel group wants a model that predicts which room bookings will be cancelled, trained on its own history of 9,000 bookings, each labelled cancelled or kept. The team merged two booking systems and removed duplicate reservation numbers. They then found 400 bookings with a blank label, and deleted those rows. Next, they set aside 15 percent of the bookings, chosen at random, before any training began, and did not show them to the training tool. AutoML then trained the model on the remaining 85 percent. What should the team do next, before using the model on live bookings?
choices: Deploy the model right away, because training has finished and the tool has already chosen the best settings
Retrain the model on all 9,000 bookings, including the set-aside ones, so it has more examples to learn from
Score the model on the 15 percent of bookings it never saw during training, and measure how often its predictions match the labels
Delete all cancelled bookings so that the cancelled and kept groups are the same size before testing
questions.why: Scoring on the set-aside bookings that the model never trained on gives an honest measure of accuracy before the model is trusted with live decisions.

questions.prompt: A freight company wants to learn from its own past shipments which orders arrived late. Which description best matches the approach of building a custom model on that data?
choices: Training a model on the company's own past shipments, each marked as on time or late, so it can find patterns that predict lateness
Writing fixed rules by hand for every route and carrier so that staff can check each order
Storing all shipment records in one place so that managers can view them in reports
Using a model that was trained in advance on general shipping data, with no records from this company
questions.why: A custom model learns from the organisation's own labelled records, here shipments marked on time or late, and then applies the patterns it finds to new orders.

questions.prompt: A network of clinics holds 12,000 appointment notes, each labelled as a no-show or as attended. The data team wants a managed approach in which the platform tries many model settings automatically and keeps the best performer, so that no one has to tune each step by hand. Which option fits this need?
choices: AutoML on the Agent Platform, which automates the trying of settings and keeps the best-performing model
Removing the labels so that the model can discover groups on its own without any correct answers
Buying a general-purpose chatbot that is used without any training on the clinic's notes
Hand-coding every layer of a neural network so that the team controls each setting
questions.why: AutoML is the managed, automated approach in which the platform tries many settings and keeps the best one, which matches the team's stated need.

questions.prompt: A warehouse records returned items with a label of damaged. Two teams use the label differently: one marks an item damaged only when it cannot be sold again, and the other marks any item with a scratch. The combined labels are used to train a model that flags damaged returns. What is the most likely result?
choices: Accuracy will rise because more examples always produce cleaner patterns, even when labels differ
The platform will automatically correct the labels during training so that both teams' meanings agree
Only the timeliness of the data is affected, and the meaning of the labels stays the same
The model will learn the mixed meaning of the label and apply it confidently to new returns, so some items may be flagged wrongly
questions.why: Inconsistent labels teach the model a blended meaning, and it then applies that meaning with confidence, which is why consistency matters as much as the choice of model.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used a ready-made AI API when building a custom model on our own data with a managed tool would make sense. Name one limit or tradeoff you would warn them about.
lessons.modelAnswer: A ready-made API is the right first choice when a general task, like reading text from an image or translating a sentence, is what we need, because it is fast and needs little data work. A custom model makes sense when our categories or decisions are specific to our business, such as ranking our own support tickets by urgency, and we have a good history of labelled examples to learn from. A managed tool like AutoML or Agent Studio handles much of the training work, so the team can focus on the data. The main tradeoff is that the custom model is only as good as its labels. If past tickets were tagged inconsistently, the model will learn those inconsistencies, so we must check completeness, accuracy and consistency before training and test on examples the model has never seen.
rubricPoints: A custom model is trained on the organization's own labelled data to fit its specific decisions.
A ready-made API suits general tasks; a custom model suits business-specific categories.
Managed tools such as AutoML or Agent Studio reduce the training and tuning work.
Data quality, especially label accuracy and consistency, limits how good the model can be.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a ready-made API and a custom model on your own data is a scenario judgement, so reasoning through an exam-style situation adds more than reading product facts.

lessons.plain: AI Hypercomputer is Google Cloud's name for the full set of computing parts used to build and run AI models. It covers the specialised chips that do the heavy arithmetic, the software that runs on those chips, the open standards that let different tools work together, and the ways a company can pay for capacity so it rents only what a job needs. Think of a professional kitchen rather than a single stove: the ovens, the prep stations, the recipes, and a booking system that lets you reserve time when you need it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team needs to train a large AI model in a week, but their ordinary servers would take three months. Before reading on, what would you change first, and what would you worry about after changing it?
lessons.teach:
AI Hypercomputer is the umbrella term Google Cloud uses for infrastructure designed for training and serving AI models. It has four parts. Accelerators are specialised chips. A GPU (graphics processing unit) contains many small processing cores that handle large numbers of similar calculations at the same time, which suits neural networks. A TPU (tensor processing unit) is Google's own accelerator built specifically for the matrix arithmetic behind machine learning. Open software and standards means widely used AI frameworks and common interfaces, so work is not tied to one machine or one vendor. Flexible consumption means choosing how you pay: on demand, reserved for a fixed term at a lower rate, or interruptible capacity that is cheaper but can be taken back.

Why it works: training a model is mostly repeating the same arithmetic over huge batches of data. Hardware that does many of these operations in parallel finishes sooner. Finishing sooner with the same power and money is the performance and efficiency case.

Worked example: a team retrains a recommendation model that needs 100 accelerator-hours. Step 1: on one accelerator, the job takes 100 hours. Step 2: on 20 accelerators working in parallel, it takes about 5 hours, assuming the work splits evenly. Step 3: they choose interruptible capacity to cut cost, so they must save checkpoints regularly, letting the job resume from the last checkpoint rather than restart.

Common mistake: assuming faster chips alone make results faster. If data loading is slow or the job is poorly split, the accelerators sit idle while you still pay for them.

Consequence in a running system: a live prediction service sized for average traffic will slow during peaks. Flexible consumption lets capacity follow demand instead of being paid for around the clock.

AI Hypercomputer pairs fast accelerators, open tooling and flexible pricing so that AI work finishes sooner and costs what it should.

questions.prompt: A genomics lab trains a model that needs 200 accelerator-hours. Step 1: on one accelerator the job takes 200 hours. Step 2: on 25 accelerators working in parallel, assuming the work splits evenly, it should take about 8 hours. Step 3: the job actually takes 14 hours, and monitoring shows the accelerators sit idle for much of that time because input data is loaded slowly. What should the team do next?
choices: Speed up the data loading so the accelerators receive batches without waiting, then measure again.
Add 25 more accelerators, which doubles the parallel capacity.
Switch the whole job to on-demand capacity so it starts sooner.
Replace the accelerators with a faster model to cut the 14 hours.
questions.why: Idle accelerators point to a feeding problem, so making data arrive faster keeps the hardware busy, whereas adding or upgrading hardware to a starved pipeline wastes money.

questions.prompt: A startup must choose between a GPU and a TPU for training a neural network. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: A TPU is a general-purpose processor for any software, while a GPU only handles graphics.
Both are interchangeable storage products that hold training checkpoints.
A GPU has many small cores doing similar calculations at once; a TPU is Google's own chip built for machine learning matrix math.
A GPU is Google's proprietary chip, and a TPU is any open-standard framework that runs on many vendors' machines.
questions.why: A GPU is defined by many small parallel cores, and a TPU is defined as Google's own accelerator built for machine learning matrix arithmetic.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a nightly model retraining job that can pause and resume without losing progress. Which purchasing option cuts cost most while fitting this job, and what must the job rely on?
choices: Interruptible capacity, provided the job saves checkpoints so it can resume.
Interruptible capacity, since the job can restart from scratch with no loss.
Reserved capacity for a fixed term, with no checkpoints needed.
On-demand capacity, since it is never taken back.
questions.why: Interruptible capacity is cheaper but can be taken back, so regular checkpoints let the job resume rather than restart.

questions.prompt: A company builds its model with a widely used open AI framework and common interfaces. What is the main benefit?
choices: It locks the company into a single pricing plan for the life of the project.
Work is not tied to one machine or one vendor, so it can be moved or run elsewhere.
It guarantees faster training than any proprietary tool.
It removes the need to save checkpoints during training.
questions.why: Open software and standards mean work is not bound to one machine or vendor, which is their purpose; they do not promise speed or remove any need for checkpoints.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what AI Hypercomputer is, why GPUs and TPUs matter for AI workloads, and one limit or tradeoff a team should weigh before choosing an interruptible or reserved option.
lessons.modelAnswer: AI Hypercomputer is Google Cloud's combined infrastructure for AI: accelerator chips, open software, and flexible ways to pay. GPUs and TPUs matter because training and serving models is mostly repeated arithmetic on large batches, and accelerators run that work in parallel, so jobs finish sooner for similar energy and cost. The tradeoff with interruptible capacity is price against reliability. It is cheaper, but the provider can reclaim it, so the job must save checkpoints and resume cleanly. Reserved capacity gives predictable availability for steady workloads but charges for time you do not use. A good choice depends on whether the job can tolerate interruption and how steady its demand is. Speed also depends on data feeding the chips fast enough, so a faster accelerator alone does not guarantee a shorter run.
rubricPoints: Defines AI Hypercomputer as a combined stack of accelerators, software, and flexible consumption
Explains that GPUs and TPUs speed AI work through parallel processing of repeated arithmetic
Names a concrete tradeoff, such as interruptible capacity being cheaper but reclaimable
Notes that data supply and job design determine whether accelerators are actually used efficiently

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product facts and concepts with no matching existing mission or planned engine, so reading the explanation is the best fit.

lessons.plain: BigQuery is a large data store where you ask questions of tables using SQL, the common language for working with rows and columns. BigQuery ML is a feature that lets you build and use machine learning models with that same SQL, so you do not have to copy data into a separate tool. Think of it as asking the database to learn a pattern from past records, such as which deliveries arrived late, and then predict the answer for new records. Because the learning happens where the data already lives, people who already know SQL can start a prediction task quickly. The catch is that the model is only as good as the table it learns from.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company keeps every past order in a database table, including whether each order was later returned. Without any special machine learning tools, what steps would you expect to take to predict whether a new order will be returned, and which step would worry you most?
lessons.teach:
BigQuery is Google Cloud's serverless data warehouse: a service for storing very large tables and running SQL queries over them without managing servers. BigQuery ML is a feature that lets you train and use machine learning models with standard SQL, so the data does not have to be exported to a separate tool. A model here is a learned pattern: you give it past examples with known outcomes, and it produces a rule for predicting the outcome for new rows. A label is the column you want to predict. Features are the columns the model learns from. Logistic regression is one model type that estimates the probability of a yes or no outcome.

Why it works: in many machine learning projects, the slow step is moving data around. When the training data already sits in a table, one SQL statement can name the model type, the label column and the feature columns. The engine trains where the data lives.

Worked example: a delivery company wants to predict whether a shipment will be late. Step one, a historical table holds past shipments with a late_flag column (true or false), plus distance_km and carrier. Step two, a CREATE MODEL statement chooses logistic regression, sets late_flag as the label, and lists distance_km and carrier as features, all selected from the historical table. Step three, BigQuery trains the model on those rows. Step four, a prediction function runs the model over this week's shipments and returns a predicted label for each one, which a query can join back to the shipment table.

Common mistake: trusting the model because it trained without an error. If late_flag was filled in wrongly for a month, or a carrier's rows were duplicated, the model learns those errors. Completeness, uniqueness and accuracy of the input matter as much as the model type.

Consequence: a dashboard that calls predictions on every refresh will display whatever the model outputs, so a quietly bad training table becomes a wrong business decision at scale. BigQuery ML puts the model next to the data, and the model's quality is limited by that data.

questions.prompt: A streaming service wants to predict whether a free-trial user will upgrade to a paid plan. Its table trial_users holds past trials with an upgraded column (true or false), minutes_watched, and device. Step one: the historical table trial_users is identified as the training source. Step two: a CREATE MODEL statement chooses logistic regression, sets upgraded as the label, and lists minutes_watched and device as the features, all drawn from trial_users. Step three: BigQuery trains the model on those rows. Step four is missing and must be supplied by the learner. It comes after training and before any predictions are run on current trial users. Which step completes the process?
choices: Rename the device column to a label so the model has two outcomes to learn from.
Run the prediction function over the current trial users only after checking the upgraded column for missing or duplicated rows, because the model learns any errors in its training table.
Delete the historical trial_users table so the model cannot be retrained on stale data.
Export trial_users to a spreadsheet so a second tool can compute the upgrade rate.
questions.why: The teaching text says a model learns whatever errors its training table contains, so checking completeness and uniqueness of the input before relying on predictions is the step that protects the result.

questions.prompt: In BigQuery ML, what is the label of a model?
choices: The SQL function that returns predictions for new rows.
The name of the dataset where the training table is stored.
The column the model is trained to predict, such as whether a booking was cancelled.
Every column in the table that the model is allowed to read during training.
questions.why: The label is the outcome column the model learns to predict, while features are the other columns it learns from.

questions.prompt: A hotel group trains a BigQuery ML model to predict cancellations. The training finishes with no errors, but a bug copied every booking from one property twice into the training table. What is the most accurate description of the risk?
choices: The model has no features left to learn from once a property's rows are repeated.
Logistic regression cannot handle duplicated rows, so the model will switch to a different model type.
The training will fail the next time it runs, so the error will be caught automatically.
The model may learn a pattern skewed toward that property, and dashboards refreshed with its predictions will show skewed results at scale.
questions.why: A clean training run does not prove the data was right; duplicated rows bias what the model learns, and a dashboard that repeatedly calls predictions will display that bias.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps its shipment records in BigQuery and wants a predictive model without moving data to another tool. Which statement best explains why BigQuery ML fits this need?
choices: It removes the need for any input data by generating synthetic shipment rows.
It guarantees the predictions will be correct regardless of how the input table was filled in.
It lets the team train and use a model with standard SQL where the table already lives, so the data does not have to be exported first.
It stores a copy of the data in a separate server so training runs faster than in the warehouse.
questions.why: BigQuery ML trains inside the warehouse with SQL, avoiding exports, but it does not generate data or guarantee accuracy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who knows SQL but not machine learning what BigQuery ML does, and name one limit or tradeoff of running a model inside the data warehouse instead of in a dedicated machine learning platform.
lessons.modelAnswer: BigQuery ML lets us build and use machine learning models using ordinary SQL inside BigQuery, so the training data never has to leave the warehouse. We write a statement that names a model type, the column we want to predict (the label), and the columns it learns from (the features), then run a prediction function over new rows. The big advantage is speed and simplicity for teams that already know SQL and keep their data in BigQuery. The tradeoff is that we get a narrower set of model types and less control over tuning than a dedicated ML platform gives. It also means the model is only as good as the tables it trains on, so we still have to check completeness, accuracy and duplicates before trusting the predictions.
rubricPoints: BigQuery ML trains and runs models using standard SQL inside BigQuery.
It removes the need to export data to a separate tool, which saves time.
It defines the label (what is predicted) and features (what the model learns from).
A tradeoff is fewer model types and less control than a dedicated ML platform.
Model quality depends on the quality of the input data, not only on the model.

suggested.rationale: A planned SQL lab would let the learner write the training and prediction statements against a small table and see how bad input rows change the result.

lessons.plain: A migration is moving a business's computing work from its own servers to a cloud provider's. Before moving anything, a team needs a shared vocabulary for what it is moving and what it will do with each piece. Think of moving house: you list everything you own, decide what to throw away, what to keep in storage for now, and how to move each item. Some boxes go as they are, some get repacked, some get a new piece of furniture bought for the new place. Cloud migration vocabulary names those choices so a team can make them one item at a time instead of treating the whole move as one big decision.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has a 15-year-old billing application that works, but nobody on the current team understands its code. Before any technical work, what would you want to know about it, and would you move it unchanged, rebuild it, or do something in between?
lessons.teach:
A workload is one job a business needs done, together with the applications, data and servers that make it run, such as a payroll system or an online order form. Migration strategy is the decision of what happens to each workload when it leaves its current home. Discovery is building an inventory: listing every server, database and application, and finding which systems depend on which. Assessment then judges each item on cost, business importance, how hard it is to move, and any rules it must follow. Only after that do you pick one of five outcomes. Retire means switch it off because nobody needs it. Retain means leave it where it is for now, for example because it was just upgraded or a regulation forbids moving it. Rehost, often called lift and shift, moves the workload to cloud virtual machines with no code changes. Replatform makes small changes that gain a clear benefit, such as swapping a self-run database for a managed database, while the core code stays the same. Refactor changes the internal code and design, for example splitting one large application into smaller services. Reimagine rebuilds the application as something new, sometimes replacing it with a different product.

Worked example: a firm has a timesheet app, a database on the same server, and a monthly report nobody has opened in two years. Discovery finds all three and shows the report reads from the database. Assessment rates the timesheet app as critical and simple to move. Step one: retire the unused report. Step two: rehost the timesheet app to a virtual machine so it moves quickly. Step three: replatform the database to a managed service, so the provider handles its backups. Refactoring can wait until the team has time to change the code safely.

Common mistake: treating the list as a ladder where the most ambitious option is always best. Reimagining a small, stable tool usually costs more than it returns.

Consequence: skipping discovery means missing a dependency. If the timesheet app contains a hard-coded address for an old server that was retired, payroll breaks on move day, even though the migration looked successful on paper.

The right outcome for each workload comes from discovery and assessment together, never from a default choice.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain has three workloads. A loyalty-points app is used by customers every day, is simple to move, and has no legal limits on where it runs. A supplier-invoice spreadsheet macro was replaced by a new tool in March, and nobody has run the macro since. A recipe-costing app runs on a self-managed database that the team wants a provider to back up, but its code is stable and the team does not want to change it. The plan so far: Step one, retire the spreadsheet macro because nothing uses it. Step two, rehost the loyalty-points app to a cloud virtual machine with no code changes. Which step completes the plan?
choices: Reimagine the loyalty-points app as a new product
Retain the recipe-costing app indefinitely with no changes
Refactor the recipe-costing app into smaller services right away
Replatform the recipe-costing app's self-managed database to a managed database service, keeping its code the same
questions.why: Moving a self-run database to a managed service so the provider handles backups is a replatform, which makes a small change for a clear gain while the core code stays the same.

questions.prompt: Which description of discovery is correct?
choices: Judging each system on cost, business importance, difficulty to move and rules it must follow
Choosing one of the five outcomes for each workload
Moving a workload onto cloud virtual machines without changing any code
Building an inventory of servers, databases and applications and finding which systems depend on which
questions.why: Discovery is the step that lists every server, database and application and maps dependencies, while judging items is assessment and moving to virtual machines is rehosting.

questions.prompt: A hospital runs a shift-scheduling app. The team rehosts it to a cloud virtual machine without running discovery. The app contains a hard-coded address for an old server that was switched off last year. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The app must be reimagined, since rehosting never allows any configuration change
The cloud provider reverses the retire decision so the old server is switched back on
The app runs faster because virtual machines remove hard-coded addresses automatically
The app may fail after the move because a hidden dependency on the retired server was never found
questions.why: Skipping discovery means a dependency such as a hard-coded address can be missed, so the workload can break on move day even though the rehost looked successful on paper.

questions.prompt: A tax-filing web app is simple to move and its team could rehost it in a week. However, a national rule requires that its records stay inside a data center in the home country, and the rule has not changed. Which outcome fits this workload?
choices: Rehost, because moving to a virtual machine is always the quickest option
Refactor, because the code should be split before any move
Retire, because the app is no longer needed once the rule applies
Retain, because the workload stays where it is for now when a rule forbids moving it
questions.why: Retain is the outcome for a workload that must stay where it is, and a binding rule overrides the fact that the app would be easy to move.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never migrated anything the difference between rehost, replatform and refactor, and name the main tradeoff of choosing rehost first for a workload that will later need to change.
lessons.modelAnswer: Rehost moves the workload to the cloud as it is, so it is the fastest and lowest-risk move, and it changes nothing in the code. Replatform keeps the code but swaps a piece of the setup for a managed equivalent, such as a managed database, which removes some maintenance work. Refactor changes the code and design so the application fits cloud features like scaling, which takes the most effort and testing. The tradeoff with rehost first is speed against cost later: the workload arrives quickly and gets the cloud's billing and hosting, but it carries its old problems with it, so the team may pay for the same inefficiency in the cloud. A good plan says when the second step will happen, so the quick move does not become permanent by accident.
rubricPoints: Rehost moves the workload with no code change and is the fastest, lowest-risk move
Replatform changes a platform piece while keeping the core code
Refactor changes the code and design, which is the most effort
Rehost first trades speed now for carrying old inefficiencies, so a later step should be planned

suggested.rationale: These are migration definitions and classifications with no listed mission or planned engine that practises them, so reading the definitions is the most direct route.

lessons.plain: Compute is the processing power that runs your software. Google Cloud offers several ways to get it, and the vocabulary is mostly about how much of the machine you manage yourself. A virtual machine is a computer simulated in software, so you control the whole operating system, like renting an unfurnished flat. A container packages an app with everything it needs to run, like a shipping box that fits any truck. Serverless means you give the provider code and it runs only when triggered, like a hotel where you never see the building staff. Knowing these words lets you match a workload to the approach that fits it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small online shop has a website that gets busy only on sale days and is quiet the rest of the year. Would you rather pay for a server that runs all year, or something that costs little when nobody is shopping? Say which you would pick and why, in one or two sentences.
lessons.teach:
A virtual machine (VM) is a computer simulated by software on shared physical hardware. You choose its operating system, memory and disks, and you manage what runs on it. Google Compute Engine provides VMs. A container is an app packaged together with its libraries and settings so it runs the same way anywhere. Putting an app into one is called containerization. Containers share the host's operating system, so they start faster and are lighter than VMs. Kubernetes is a system that schedules and runs many containers across a group of machines, restarting failed ones. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) is Google's managed Kubernetes service. A microservice is a small, separately deployed piece of an application that does one job and talks to other pieces over the network. Serverless computing means you deploy code and the provider handles servers, scaling and billing per request. Cloud Run runs containers this way. A managed service is one where the provider runs the underlying software for you, including patching and backups.

Autoscaling adds or removes instances as load changes. Load balancing spreads incoming requests across several instances so none is overloaded and failed ones can be skipped. Spot VMs are spare Compute Engine capacity sold at a steep discount, but Google can reclaim them with short notice, so they suit interruptible batch work rather than a single critical server.

Worked example: a photo-resizing job runs hourly and takes four minutes. Step one, package the resizer as a container. Step two, run it serverless so nothing is billed between runs. Step three, if a run is interrupted, retry it. Common mistake: choosing Spot VMs for a checkout service because they are cheap, then losing live customers when a VM is reclaimed. Consequence: a set of VMs with no load balancer goes down whenever one machine fails, while balanced instances keep serving. The right choice depends on how much you want to manage and how much interruption the work can tolerate.

questions.prompt: A tax software vendor runs a quarterly reconciliation that takes six hours on one large virtual machine (VM, a computer simulated by software on shared hardware). The job saves a checkpoint, meaning a snapshot of its progress, to durable storage every ten minutes, so it can resume after an interruption. Step one: move the job to Spot VMs, which are spare capacity sold at a steep discount that the provider can reclaim with short notice, because the job can resume from checkpoints. Step two: ____. Which step completes the plan?
choices: Attach a load balancer across the Spot VMs so incoming requests are spread between them.
Replace the VM with a managed database so the provider handles patching and backups.
Configure the job to restart from its most recent checkpoint whenever a Spot VM is reclaimed.
Increase the memory on each Spot VM so each six-hour run finishes faster.
questions.why: Because Spot VMs can be reclaimed at short notice, the job must be set to resume from its last checkpoint, which is what keeps interruptible batch work from losing hours of progress.

questions.prompt: A nightly price-update tool is bundled with its libraries and settings so it behaves the same on a developer laptop and on a production server. What is this packaging approach called?
choices: Containerization, packaging an app with its dependencies so it runs the same anywhere
Spot provisioning, buying spare capacity at a discount
Serverless deployment, where the provider handles servers and scaling
Microservice decomposition, splitting the app into small separately deployed pieces
questions.why: Containerization is the term for packaging an app with its libraries and settings so it runs the same way in any environment, which is exactly what the tool does.

questions.prompt: A retailer's order-status service runs on four identical VMs with no load balancer. One VM fails, and customers using that machine see errors until someone restarts it. Which change best addresses this failure case?
choices: Add more memory to each of the four VMs so they are less likely to fail.
Schedule the four VMs to stop overnight to cut costs.
Place a load balancer in front of the four VMs so requests are spread across them and failed instances are skipped.
Move all four VMs to Spot VMs to reduce the monthly bill.
questions.why: A load balancer spreads requests across several instances and skips failed ones, so one machine failing no longer takes the service down; the other options add cost, risk or don't address the single-point problem.

questions.prompt: A startup needs a small image-resizing function that runs for a few seconds each time a user uploads a photo. The team wants to pay nothing while idle and does not want to patch or manage any servers. Which approach fits best?
choices: A dedicated VM that runs all day, so it is always ready for uploads.
Spot VMs with no retry logic, since they are the cheapest option.
A serverless container service that is billed per request and scales to zero when idle.
A self-managed Kubernetes cluster whose nodes the team patches itself.
questions.why: Serverless computing bills per request and handles servers and scaling, which matches a short, upload-triggered job with no idle cost and no server management; the other options either cost money while idle or require the team to run servers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a virtual machine, a container and a serverless function, and name one limit or tradeoff of each, as you would in a design review.
lessons.modelAnswer: A virtual machine gives you a whole simulated computer with its own operating system, so you have the most control and also the most to patch and manage. A container packages one app with its dependencies and shares the host's operating system, so it starts quickly and packs densely, but it is less isolated than a VM and needs a platform such as Kubernetes to run at scale. Serverless means you ship code and the provider runs and scales it, billing per request. That removes server work, but runs are usually short, you have less control over the environment, and cold starts can add latency. So a long-running app that needs custom OS settings suits a VM, a steady packaged service suits containers, and a bursty short task suits serverless. Each choice trades control against operational effort.
rubricPoints: A virtual machine is a full simulated computer you manage, with the most control and the most upkeep.
A container packages an app with its dependencies and shares the host OS, so it starts fast but needs a platform to run at scale.
Serverless runs code on demand and bills per use, but imposes limits on run time and control of the environment.
Each option trades control against operational effort, and the right answer depends on the workload.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a fitting compute approach and explaining why the near-miss fails is exam-style situational reasoning that no current mission teaches directly.

lessons.plain: A virtual machine is a computer that exists as software inside a large data centre run by someone else. Google Cloud's Compute Engine lets a company rent these machines by the hour, choosing the operating system, memory and processor count, and starting or stopping them on demand. The business case is the argument that this is worth doing: it lets a company stop buying and babysitting physical servers, move existing applications without rewriting them, and pay for capacity that matches real demand. Knowing when that argument holds, and when a different approach would serve better, is the skill being taught here.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs a fifteen-year-old accounting program that only works on one specific old operating system and needs no code changes. Before any teaching, what would you guess is the strongest reason to move it to the cloud as a virtual machine rather than rewrite it for a newer approach?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A virtual machine (VM) is a software-defined computer: it has its own operating system, memory and disk, but it runs on shared physical hardware in a provider's data centre. Compute Engine is Google Cloud's service for creating and running these VMs. A business case is the reasoning that shows a choice pays off in money, speed or reduced risk.

Why the VM option works: the application still sees a normal server, so the team can move it largely unchanged. That avoids the cost and risk of rewriting code, and it removes the expense of buying hardware, waiting for purchase orders, and maintaining racks, cooling and power. Capacity can be added or removed in minutes, and you pay for the time the machine runs.

Worked example: a logistics firm runs a reporting server in its own server room. Step one, the hardware is five years old and due replacement. Step two, the team prices a new physical box plus cooling and maintenance. Step three, a VM of the same size is created in Compute Engine and the software is copied across unchanged. Step four, the reporting job only needs the machine during working hours, so the team stops it overnight. The case rests on avoided hardware purchase, no rewrite, and paying only for running hours.

Common mistake: treating a VM as automatically cheaper. A machine left running at full size all month, or sized far larger than the workload needs (the practice of matching size to real need is called right-sizing), can cost more than the old server. The saving depends on right-sizing and switching off idle machines.

Consequence: because you pay for uptime, a forgotten VM keeps billing. A VM you run also needs its operating system kept patched (installing security updates) and its data backed up, so the business case must include that staff effort.

The VM approach is the strongest business case when a workload must stay close to how it runs today; it is a weaker case when the application could be redesigned to run on managed services that need less upkeep.

questions.prompt: A regional accounts firm runs a legacy bookkeeping application that must stay unchanged for audit reasons. The business case is worked through in four steps, and step four is missing. Step one: the firm's on-premises server is due for replacement. Step two: the team prices a new physical server, plus cooling and maintenance. Step three: the team creates a Compute Engine VM sized to the application's measured peak, copies the software across unchanged, and schedules the VM to run only during office hours. Step four: ___. Which completes the case?
choices: The team assumes the VM costs the same as the old server because the software is unchanged.
The team adds the staff time needed to keep the VM's operating system patched and its data backed up to the cost comparison.
The team removes the need for operating system updates because the cloud provider patches every VM automatically.
The team keeps the VM running around the clock so the saving never depends on someone remembering to stop it.
questions.why: Because a VM you run still needs its operating system patched and its data backed up, that staff effort belongs in the business case, and only option C names this ongoing work.

questions.prompt: A managed service is a cloud service where the provider runs the underlying machines and handles most of the upkeep for you. A startup has a small app that could be rebuilt to run on a managed service instead of a VM. Based only on the idea that a VM is a weaker business case when the app could be redesigned, which statement is most accurate?
choices: A VM is always the cheapest option, so the rebuild is never worth considering.
The VM is weaker only if the app needs more than one operating system.
Keeping the app on a VM is weaker because the team would still carry the upkeep that a managed service would remove.
Redesigning the app always costs more than running a VM, so the VM case is always stronger.
questions.why: The teaching text says the VM case is weaker when a redesign to managed services would reduce upkeep, which is the point made in option B.

questions.prompt: A media company moved a video-encoding server to a Compute Engine VM. Its monthly cloud bill is now higher than the old physical server's running costs. Using the common-mistake idea from the teaching text, what is the most likely explanation?
choices: The software had to be copied across, which doubles the bill for the first month only.
The VM hardware is slower than the old server, so the work takes longer and costs more.
Compute Engine charges for stored data regardless of whether the VM is running.
The VM was left running at full size all month, and nobody checked whether it needed to be that large or running at all.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a machine left running at full size, or sized larger than needed, can cost more than the old server, which matches option C.

questions.prompt: A retail chain runs an order-tracking application on a VM. The application needs no code changes to move to Compute Engine. Which combination best describes the business benefits the chain can legitimately claim, based only on the teaching text?
choices: It avoids rewriting the code and avoids waiting for hardware purchase orders, and it pays only for the time the machine runs.
It removes the need for any staff effort, because capacity adds itself automatically.
It guarantees a lower bill than any physical server, whatever size the VM is and however long it runs.
It avoids all operating system maintenance and needs no backups, because the VM is cloud-hosted.
questions.why: The teaching text names avoided rewrites, no hardware purchase wait, and paying for running time as the core benefits, which is exactly what option A states.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who thinks every workload should move to the cloud as a VM on Compute Engine when running VMs is the right business case and when it is not. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of the VM approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Running VMs on Compute Engine makes sense when a workload must stay close to how it runs today, for example an old application that needs a specific operating system and cannot be rewritten cheaply. The case rests on avoiding hardware purchases and data-centre upkeep, moving quickly without code changes, and paying only for the hours the machines run. The main limit is that we still own the operating system: we patch it, back it up, and size it correctly, and a machine left running oversized or forgotten keeps costing money. If the application could instead run on managed services that handle much of that upkeep, the VM case weakens, so I would compare the staff effort and running cost of both before deciding.
rubricPoints: Defines a VM as a software computer running on shared provider hardware
States the core benefits: avoided hardware purchases and upkeep, and no code rewrite needed
Names a real tradeoff, such as the team still owning patching, backups and sizing
Explains that cost depends on right-sizing and switching off idle machines, and that a managed alternative may be better for some workloads

suggested.rationale: Defending a VM business case against a near-miss alternative is best practised by explaining the tradeoffs aloud, since no listed mission covers cloud compute economics.

lessons.plain: Modern application development means building software as several smaller pieces that run on platforms able to grow, shrink and recover on their own, often using services that a cloud provider runs for you. Think of a food truck compared with a restaurant with a fixed kitchen: the truck can add help for a festival, move to a new spot, and keep serving if one burner breaks. The value is not that the code is fancier. It is that teams can change one part without touching the rest, launch features faster, pay roughly in step with real use, handle busy and quiet periods, survive partial failures, and spend less human time on routine upkeep.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small online shop sells almost nothing for eleven months a year, then gets ten times its normal traffic for one week in December. Before any teaching, what would you change about how the shop is built so it does not need to pay for peak capacity all year, and what risk would your change introduce?
lessons.teach:
Modern application development means splitting an application into smaller services that talk to each other, and running them on platforms that adjust capacity automatically. A managed service is one the cloud provider operates for you, handling patching, backups and much of the scaling, so your team configures it rather than running the software itself. Scalability is the ability to add or remove capacity as demand changes. Resilience is the ability to keep working, perhaps in a reduced form, when one part fails. A queue is a holding area where requests wait until a worker is ready to process them, which lets a slow or broken part fall behind without losing work.

Worked example: a ticket-sales site expects a spike when tickets for a concert open. Step one: the web front end runs on a service that adds instances as requests rise and removes them when traffic falls. Step two: when a buyer clicks purchase, the order is placed on a queue instead of being processed inline. Step three: a payment worker takes orders from the queue at a pace the payment provider allows. Step four: the database is a managed service with automatic backups. During the spike, the front end scales out, the queue absorbs the surge, and the team pays for extra capacity only while it is used.

A common mistake is assuming that modern means automatically cheaper. A service set to keep a large minimum number of instances running all month, or a design that calls many services for every page view, can cost more than a plain fixed server. Savings come from matching capacity to demand and from removing idle time.

In a running system, the queue is what keeps the sale from failing when the payment worker is briefly down: orders wait rather than vanish, though the backlog must be watched so it does not grow faster than it drains.

questions.prompt: A podcast host runs an episode-processing pipeline. Step one: the upload service accepts an audio file and places a processing job on a queue instead of converting the file inline. Step two: transcoding workers run on a service that adds workers when the queue grows long and removes them when it empties. Step three: [missing step]. Step four: finished audio files are kept in a managed storage service that handles backups. On the day a new season launches, a sudden wave of uploads arrives. Which completion correctly fills step three?
choices: The upload service waits for each conversion to finish before accepting the next file, so the queue never holds more than one job.
Every transcoding worker is kept running at full size all month so that no job ever has to wait in line.
The team deletes any job that has waited more than a few seconds, so the queue stays short during the rush.
Each worker takes jobs from the queue at a pace it can sustain, so a burst of uploads builds a backlog that shrinks as the workers keep up.
questions.why: Workers pulling from the queue at a pace they can sustain lets the queue absorb the burst, which is the protective role the teaching text gives a queue, while the other choices either tie uploads to conversion, pay for idle capacity, or throw away work.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a managed service?
choices: A holding area where requests wait until a worker is ready to process them.
A rule that caps how many instances a service may run at the same time.
A service your team must patch, back up and scale by hand, so you control every detail of the software.
A cloud service the provider operates for you, handling patching, backups and much of the scaling, while your team only configures it.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a managed service as one the provider operates for you, so your team configures it instead of running the software itself.

questions.prompt: A charity's donation website keeps working in reduced form when its receipt-printing component fails, because donations are still recorded and the receipts are sent later. Which property does this describe?
choices: Scalability, the ability to add or remove capacity as demand changes.
Resilience, the ability to keep working, perhaps in reduced form, when one part fails.
A queue, a holding area where requests wait for a ready worker.
Automatic cost optimization, which removes all idle time from the system.
questions.why: Continuing to work in reduced form when one part fails is the teaching text's definition of resilience, and the other options name different ideas.

questions.prompt: A small nonprofit moves its event-signup form to a platform configured to keep twenty instances running at all times. Its traffic is steady at about two requests a minute. Why might this design cost more than a plain fixed server?
choices: Queues cannot be used with a small number of requests, so the platform must run extra instances.
A large minimum number of instances runs all month even when demand is low, so paying for idle capacity can exceed the cost of one fixed server.
The platform scales out automatically, which means the nonprofit cannot control its spending at all.
Managed services always charge more than fixed servers, regardless of configuration.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that keeping a large minimum of instances running all month can cost more than a plain fixed server, because savings come from matching capacity to demand and removing idle time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only run one fixed server for their company's website why moving to a set of managed, scalable services can be worth it, and name one real limit or tradeoff of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The main reason is that the website's load is uneven, and a fixed server must be sized for the busiest day, so it sits mostly idle the rest of the year. With managed services, the front end can add instances during a sale and remove them afterward, and the provider handles patching and backups, so our small team spends less time on upkeep. Splitting the system also means one part can fail without taking everything down, because orders can wait on a queue. The tradeoff is that the design gets more complicated: we now have several services to monitor, network calls that can fail between them, and a bill that depends on usage, so a misconfigured minimum instance count or a chatty design can cost more than the old server did. We need to watch both the queue backlog and the monthly spend.
rubricPoints: Defines scalability or elasticity as capacity that follows demand, so cost tracks real use
Explains that managed services shift routine operations such as patching and backups to the provider
Describes resilience as keeping parts of the system working when one part fails, using queues or loose coupling
Names a real tradeoff such as added complexity, distributed failure points, or usage-based cost surprises

suggested.rationale: This objective is a judgement about why an architecture is valuable, so being able to explain the value and its limits back is the core skill.

lessons.plain: A container packages an application together with everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same on a laptop, a test server, or in the cloud. Running one container is easy. Running hundreds of them, restarting the ones that crash, adding more when traffic rises, and spreading them across machines is hard work. Kubernetes is open-source software that coordinates this for you. Google Kubernetes Engine, called GKE, is Google's managed version: Google runs the core management parts of Kubernetes so your team can focus on the applications instead of the machinery underneath them. The business case is fewer manual operations, faster and safer releases, and better use of the servers you pay for.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs on one server. At 3 a.m. that server crashes and nobody is awake. What would you want to happen automatically, and what would someone have to do by hand today to fix it?
lessons.teach:
A container image is a sealed package holding an application and its dependencies. A container is a running copy of that image. A cluster is a group of machines, called nodes, that share the work. Kubernetes is the software that decides which containers run on which nodes, and keeps them running. You describe the desired state, for example run six copies of the positions service, and a control loop keeps checking reality and correcting any gap. The control plane is the management part of the cluster that makes these decisions. In GKE, Google operates the control plane and handles its upgrades, which is what the word managed means here. Your team still chooses the nodes, the applications and the settings.

Worked example. A booking service normally runs three copies. At lunch, CPU use across the copies rises above the target you set. The autoscaler adds replicas, and the scheduler places them on nodes with spare room. Later, one copy crashes. The control loop sees five running instead of six and starts a replacement within seconds. When traffic falls, the extra copies are removed and you stop paying for idle capacity.

Common mistake. Teams assume GKE is automatically cheaper. You still pay for the nodes, and a team without container skills can spend more running a complex cluster than running one simple managed serverless service. Consequence in a live system: a bad rollout with no limits on how many copies may be replaced at once can take every copy down together, so rolling update settings matter as much as the cluster itself.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs its seat-hold service as 8 copies on version 2. You set the desired state to version 3 and configure the rollout so that at most 2 copies are replaced at any one time. Step 1: the control plane, which Google operates, accepts version 3 as the new desired state. Step 2: the rollout stops 2 version-2 copies and starts 2 version-3 copies. Step 3 is missing from this trace and you must fill it in. Step 4: the rollout moves on to the next pair of copies, and the process repeats until all 8 run version 3.
choices: The control loop checks that the new copies are running before the next pair is replaced.
The control plane is shut down so that upgrades cannot conflict with running copies.
The autoscaler removes every copy so that the rollout starts from zero.
All 8 version-2 copies are deleted at once so the nodes can be reset.
questions.why: The control loop keeps comparing reality with the desired state, so it confirms the new copies are running before the rollout continues, which keeps most of the service available.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the control loop's job in a Kubernetes cluster such as GKE?
choices: It checks the actual state of the cluster against the desired state and corrects any gap.
It writes the application code that the team deploys into containers.
It stores the container images that the nodes download.
It sets the price the company pays for each node per hour.
questions.why: The teaching text describes the control loop as repeatedly comparing reality with the desired state you described and correcting any difference.

questions.prompt: A small firm runs one internal expense-form app. It has steady, low traffic, and its team has no container experience. Based on the business case for GKE, which option is the better fit to consider first?
choices: A managed serverless service, because a simple app with no container skills can cost less than running a complex cluster
Three separate GKE clusters, one per office, so that each office has its own control plane
A self-built Kubernetes cluster on rented machines, because it avoids paying Google for the control plane
A GKE cluster with several node pools, because managed means the team needs no container skills
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a team without container skills can spend more running a complex cluster than running one simple managed serverless service, so the serverless option is the better first consideration.

questions.prompt: A team sets its rolling update so that it has no limit on how many copies may be replaced at once. A new release has a fault. What is the most likely consequence in the live system?
choices: The fault is caught automatically before any copy is changed, so users never notice.
The autoscaler adds more nodes, so the fault costs more money but never causes downtime.
Only one copy is affected, and the control loop repairs it before any traffic is lost.
Every copy can be taken down together, so the service may go fully offline, which is why rollout limits matter as much as the cluster itself.
questions.why: Without a limit on simultaneous replacements, a faulty release can replace all copies together, taking the whole service down, as the teaching text warns.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only run apps on single virtual machines why moving our services to GKE could be worth the business cost. Name one limit or tradeoff we must weigh before choosing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: GKE gives us a managed way to run many containers across a group of machines. Instead of our engineers restarting crashed apps, adding servers by hand, or patching every machine, Kubernetes keeps the declared number of copies running, replaces failed ones, and scales with demand. Google runs the management layer and its upgrades, so we spend less time on routine operations and more on product work. Releases can roll out gradually, which reduces the risk of an outage during deployment. The tradeoff is that we still pay for the worker nodes whether or not they are busy, and Kubernetes adds concepts our team must learn. For a single small app with light, occasional traffic, a simpler serverless option may cost less and take less effort to run, so the choice depends on how many services we run and how often they change.
rubricPoints: GKE is Google's managed Kubernetes, which runs containers and handles scaling and self-healing.
The business value is reduced manual operations, faster and safer releases, and better resource use.
Google operates the control plane, but the organization still pays for and manages its nodes and applications.
A tradeoff is added complexity and skills need, and a simpler option may fit small or occasional workloads better.

suggested.rationale: A workload-choice scenario asks the learner to pick GKE and reject a near-miss such as single virtual machines or serverless, which practice reasoning builds more than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Serverless compute means you hand the provider a piece of code or a container and it runs it for you, without you buying, patching or watching any machines. Cloud Run runs containers that answer web or API requests, and Cloud Run functions runs small pieces of code that react to events such as a file upload. The business case is simple: you pay mainly for the work actually done, the platform adds capacity when demand rises and removes it when demand falls, and your team spends its time on the product rather than on servers. It is like taking taxis instead of owning a car: you pay per trip, and someone else looks after the vehicle.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small internal tool gets almost no traffic for weeks, then a burst of heavy use on the last day of each month. Would you rather pay for a server that runs all month, or pay only while requests are being handled? Why?
lessons.teach:
Serverless compute is a model where the cloud provider owns the servers, the operating system and the capacity planning, and you are billed for the work your code does. It does not mean there are no servers; it means you do not manage them. Cloud Run runs a container, which is a packaged application with everything it needs, and serves web or API requests. Cloud Run functions runs a single function in response to an event, such as a message arriving on a queue or a file landing in storage.

Why the model pays off: Cloud Run can scale to zero, meaning it runs no instances when nobody is calling, and it starts more instances when traffic rises. Autoscaling is this automatic adding and removing of copies of your code. Billing follows usage, so an idle service costs little. Your team also skips patching machines, which is a large part of operational efficiency.

Worked example: an internal endpoint that resizes uploaded images. Overnight it receives zero requests, so zero instances run and no compute is billed. At noon, 200 uploads arrive each second. Step 1: the platform sees queued requests and starts instances. Step 2: each instance handles several requests at once, up to its configured concurrency, which is the number of requests one instance serves simultaneously. Step 3: when the burst ends, instances are removed and billing for them stops.

Common mistake: assuming serverless is always cheaper. A workload that runs at a steady high level all day can cost less on a reserved virtual machine, and a long-running job may exceed the time limit that a request-based service allows. Another mistake is ignoring retries: an event-driven function may run twice for the same message, so its work must be safe to repeat.

Consequence: if many scaled-out instances all open database connections at once, the database can run out of connections and fail even though the compute layer scaled correctly. Limits must be planned on both sides.

questions.prompt: A ticket-resale company runs a Cloud Run API that holds seats for buyers. Overnight it receives no requests, so no instances run and no compute is billed. At 9 a.m., 60 requests per second arrive, and each instance is configured for a concurrency of 20, meaning one instance serves up to 20 requests at the same time. Step 1: the platform sees the queued requests and starts instances. Step 2: at 20 requests per instance, the 60 requests per second need about 3 instances. Step 3: ___ Which step completes the trace?
choices: The database automatically receives extra connections from Cloud Run.
When traffic drops, the instances are removed and billing for them stops.
Billing for the instances continues until someone manually deletes them.
Each request is split across all instances so that each one finishes faster.
questions.why: Billing follows usage in this model, so once the platform removes idle instances after traffic falls, their billing stops; the other choices misread autoscaling, concurrency, or how connections work.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches serverless compute as this course defines it?
choices: You rent a fixed virtual machine and pay the same amount whether it is busy or idle.
The provider owns the servers, operating system and capacity planning, and you pay for the work your code does.
You patch and size the machines yourself, but the platform bills you per request.
There are no servers involved, so the provider has nothing to run.
questions.why: The course defines serverless as the provider owning the servers, operating system and capacity planning, with billing tied to the work your code does, while servers still exist behind the scenes.

questions.prompt: A function triggered by messages on a queue occasionally receives the same message twice. What must the function's work be?
choices: Completed in under a fixed number of seconds.
Limited to one instance at a time to prevent retries.
Safe to repeat, so a second run does not cause a duplicate effect.
Run on a reserved machine so that retries are cheaper.
questions.why: An event-driven function may run more than once for the same message, so its work must be safe to repeat; the other choices do not address duplicate runs.

questions.prompt: During a sale, a team's Cloud Run service scales out to 300 instances, and the database then fails because it runs out of connections. Which reading is best?
choices: The team should remove autoscaling so that instance counts stay fixed at one.
Scaling worked as designed, but instance counts and database connection capacity were not planned together.
Cloud Run scaled incorrectly and should be replaced with a reserved virtual machine.
The database is unrelated, so the fault must be in the image resizing code.
questions.why: The compute layer scaling correctly can still overwhelm the database's connection limit, so limits must be planned on both sides, which is the point the teaching text makes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why a team might choose Cloud Run over a virtual machine for a new internal API, and name one limit or tradeoff they should accept with that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick Cloud Run for a new internal API because we would stop maintaining operating systems and patching servers, and the service would scale from zero to many instances and back, so we only pay while requests arrive. A virtual machine stays on unless we manage its schedule, and we would own its patching, scaling and failover. The tradeoff to accept is that each request has a time limit and new instances can take a moment to start, so latency-sensitive calls may notice cold starts, which are delays while a fresh instance boots. We also must make any retried work safe, and we should check database connection limits, since many instances can open connections at once. If traffic were constant and heavy all day, I would re-run the cost comparison before assuming serverless wins.
rubricPoints: Explains that serverless removes server management and bills mainly for actual use, including scale to zero
Contrasts with a virtual machine, which the team must patch, scale and keep running
Names a real limit such as request time limits, cold starts or per-request concurrency
Notes that steady, heavy, always-on workloads may cost less on other options, so the choice needs checking

suggested.rationale: Choosing between serverless, virtual machines and containers in a described situation is best learned by reasoning through a scenario, and no listed mission covers this business case directly.

lessons.plain: Many companies do not run everything in one cloud. Some keep systems in their own data centres, some use more than one cloud provider, and some have data spread across all of them. Google Cloud offers a few products designed to work across these mixed settings, not only inside Google's own data centres. This lesson covers five of them: a database you can run outside Google Cloud, a way to analyse data where it already sits in another cloud, a way to manage many Kubernetes clusters from one place, a fully managed database that lives inside Google Cloud, and a tool that turns data into dashboards and reports. The core skill is matching each product to where the workload and its data actually live.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company keeps its customer sales records in a database running in its own server room, and its marketing data in storage belonging to a different cloud provider. Leadership wants one dashboard that answers questions across both, without copying every file into Google Cloud first. Which kind of Google Cloud product would you expect to help, and why might copying everything first be a problem?
lessons.teach:
Multicloud means using more than one cloud provider. Hybrid means running some workloads in your own data centre (on-premises) and others in the cloud. The products in this group are built so Google Cloud tools still work when part of your estate sits outside Google's data centres.

AlloyDB Omni is a database engine compatible with PostgreSQL, a widely used open-source relational database. Compatible means existing applications and queries work with little change. Because it can run on your own hardware or another cloud, it suits a database that must stay on-premises. Cloud SQL is a managed database service: Google runs the server, patching and backups, but only inside Google Cloud. If the data must stay in a rack you own, Cloud SQL is the wrong answer, even though it is easier to operate.

BigQuery Omni runs BigQuery's SQL analytics on data stored in other clouds, such as AWS or Azure. Worked example: a marketing team has two terabytes of campaign logs in another cloud's storage. Step 1: an analyst writes one SQL query in BigQuery. Step 2: the query runs where the logs sit. Step 3: only the small summary result returns to Google Cloud. The team never copied the full dataset. The common mistake is assuming the data must be moved first; it does not, though results still need to be sized sensibly.

GKE Enterprise is a management layer for Kubernetes, the system that schedules containers across many machines. It groups clusters into a fleet and applies one set of policies across clusters in Google Cloud, other clouds and on-premises.
