Looker is a business intelligence platform: it defines business metrics once in a modelling layer and produces dashboards, and it can connect to databases outside Google Cloud.

The consequence of a poor match is real. A product that cannot reach the data where it lives forces copy pipelines that are slow, costly and create a second store of sensitive data to protect. Choose the product that fits where the data and workload already run.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs its shipment-tracking app on a PostgreSQL database inside its own warehouse, because a regulator requires that database to stay on hardware the firm controls. The team wants to keep the app's existing SQL unchanged. Step 1: they confirm the app uses only standard PostgreSQL features. Step 2: they install AlloyDB Omni on the warehouse server, which is a PostgreSQL-compatible engine that can run on the firm's own hardware. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the app keeps running with little or no change to its queries.
choices: Rewrite every query into a proprietary dialect supported only by Google Cloud
Export the tracking data nightly to a spreadsheet that the app reads
Point the existing application connection settings at the AlloyDB Omni instance on the warehouse server
Move the warehouse data into Cloud SQL so Google runs the backups
questions.why: Because AlloyDB Omni is compatible with PostgreSQL and runs on the firm's own server, the app only needs its connection settings pointed at the new engine, which is the step that makes the rest of the flow work.

questions.prompt: A hospital group must keep a PostgreSQL patient-records database inside its own data centre for legal reasons. Which Google Cloud product fits best, and why is Cloud SQL the near miss?
choices: Looker, because it can connect to databases outside Google Cloud and build dashboards
Cloud SQL, because it is managed and easier to operate than running a database yourself
AlloyDB Omni, because it can run on the hospital's own hardware while staying PostgreSQL-compatible
BigQuery Omni, because it can run SQL on data stored in another cloud
questions.why: AlloyDB Omni runs on the hospital's own hardware and is PostgreSQL-compatible, while Cloud SQL only runs inside Google Cloud, so it would break the on-premises requirement.

questions.prompt: A bank keeps 400 GB of card-transaction logs in an object store in another cloud. Its analysts want to run SQL summaries in BigQuery without creating a second copy of the logs. Which choice best describes the approach, and what is the common mistake to avoid?
choices: Use BigQuery Omni so the SQL runs where the logs sit and only the summary results return, avoiding a full copy
Use Cloud SQL and import the logs as tables, because it is the managed option for analytics
Copy all 400 GB into BigQuery first, because BigQuery can only query data stored inside Google Cloud
Use Looker to export the logs into dashboards, because Looker stores the raw data itself
questions.why: BigQuery Omni runs the SQL where the data already lives, so the full dataset need not be moved; copying first is the mistake this approach avoids.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs Kubernetes clusters in Azure, in its own data centre and in Google Cloud, and wants one set of security policies applied across all of them. Which product should it choose?
choices: Looker, because it defines business metrics once and produces dashboards
Cloud SQL, because it manages database patching and backups
BigQuery Omni, because it runs analytics on data stored in other clouds
GKE Enterprise, because it groups clusters into a fleet and applies one policy set across clouds and on-premises
questions.why: GKE Enterprise is the management layer for Kubernetes that spans multiple environments, while the other products handle databases, dashboards or analytics rather than cluster policy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose AlloyDB Omni over Cloud SQL, and name one limit or tradeoff of running it yourself.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick AlloyDB Omni when the PostgreSQL database has to run somewhere other than Google Cloud, such as our own data centre or another provider, perhaps because of data residency rules or latency to local systems. Cloud SQL is the better default when the database can live inside Google Cloud, because Google handles patching, backups and failover for us. The tradeoff with Omni is that we take on more of the operating work: we provision the hosts, keep the software updated, monitor it and pay for that infrastructure ourselves. So the decision comes down to where the data must sit, weighed against how much operations work the team is willing to own.
rubricPoints: AlloyDB Omni can run outside Google Cloud, while Cloud SQL runs only inside it.
The choice is driven by where the data must stay, not by which product is easiest.
Running Omni shifts patching, backups and host operations onto the customer.
A good answer names a concrete cost or operations burden of self-running the database.

suggested.rationale: This objective is a product catalogue of where each service runs, which is best learned by reading and matching products to placement needs, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: An API, short for application programming interface, is a published set of rules for asking a program to do a task. Think of a restaurant menu: it lists what you may order, the format to order in, and what comes back, so you never need to see the kitchen. Businesses expose APIs so partners and customers can plug their own software into a service. Some charge for that access, which is called monetizing the API. This lesson explains what an API is and why a company might open one up to the public and sell access to it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A weather app on your phone shows a forecast it did not compute itself. Without looking anything up, what do you think the app most likely does to get that forecast, and what would the weather company gain by letting outside apps do the same thing?
lessons.teach:
An API, short for application programming interface, is a published set of rules for asking a program to do a task. It names the requests you may send, the data each one needs, and the shape of the answer that comes back. An endpoint is one address in that set, such as a route that returns a price estimate. A key is a secret token a caller sends so the provider knows who is asking. An API works because the caller needs only the rules, not the provider's internal code, so two organizations can connect without sharing their internals. A public-facing API is one open to outside developers or customers, and monetizing it means charging for access, often per call or through paid tiers.

Worked example: a bike-share company publishes an endpoint that quotes the cost of a ride. Step 1: a partner's app sends a request containing a start point, an end point and its key. Step 2: a gateway checks that the key is valid and that the partner still has calls left in its quota. Step 3: the pricing service computes the fare and returns it as structured data. Step 4: the partner's app shows the fare to its own user. Step 5: the company records the call, which becomes the basis for a monthly bill.

The business case is reach and revenue. Partners extend the company's service into places it could not build alone, developers adopt a free tier and then pay as their volume grows, and call data shows which features customers actually use.

Common mistake: treating a public API as a website with a free door. Without keys, quotas and rate limits, one client stuck in a loop can consume capacity meant for everyone else.

In a running system, the rate limit is what keeps one misbehaving partner from slowing the service for paying customers.

questions.prompt: Harbourline Ferries publishes a public endpoint that returns the number of free seats on a ferry route. Each partner key is allowed 60 calls per minute, which is a rate limit: a cap on how many calls one key may make in a set window of time. The steps for one call are: Step 1, a travel-booking site sends a request containing a route ID and its key. Step 2, the provider confirms the key is valid. Step 3 is missing and you must supply it: the gateway, which is the front door that sits in front of the service and applies these checks, counts this key's calls in the current minute and finds that the partner has already made 60, so this 61st call is over the limit. Step 4, the partner's app receives a refusal and waits before retrying. What must happen at Step 3?
choices: The gateway turns the call away because it is over the per-minute limit, so the seat lookup never runs.
The gateway deletes the partner's key after the first call that exceeds the limit.
The service runs the seat lookup, then withholds the result from the partner.
The gateway forwards the call to the next minute's window and processes it later.
questions.why: A rate limit is enforced before the service does any work, so an over-limit call is refused at the gateway and the lookup never runs, which protects capacity for other callers.

questions.prompt: A freight company says its API lets partners connect without seeing its internal code. Which statement best describes what the API itself is?
choices: A published set of rules that names the requests a caller may send, the data each request needs, and the shape of the reply.
The full source code of the company's pricing service, shared with partners so they can copy the logic.
A secret token that tells the provider which customer is calling, and nothing more.
A single internet address where a partner's app is stored and run on the company's servers.
questions.why: An API is the published rulebook for making requests and reading replies, which is why callers can connect without access to the provider's internals.

questions.prompt: A weather-data firm offers a free tier of 1,000 calls a month and paid tiers above that. Which outcome best matches the business case for publishing this as a public API?
choices: Developers on the free tier grow their call volume and move to paid tiers, and call records show which features they use.
The firm avoids all running costs, because partners pay the hosting bills for the servers that answer their calls.
Keys stop being needed, because paid tiers replace the need to confirm who is calling the service at all.
The API has to stay private, so that competitors cannot learn what price the firm charges per call.
questions.why: The business case is reach and revenue: free use leads to paid use as volume grows, and call data shows which features customers value.

questions.prompt: A transit agency publishes a public API for live bus arrival times, but it issues no keys and sets no rate limits. Which failure is most likely to happen?
choices: Each partner will need the agency's source code before it can connect, because the rules are not published.
One client stuck in a retry loop can consume capacity meant for other riders' apps, and nothing limits it.
Partner apps will show wrong fares, because the response format has no structure that a program can read.
The agency will be unable to publish new endpoints later, because the API has no version history to build on.
questions.why: Without keys and rate limits nothing stops a single misbehaving client from using shared capacity, which is the central risk of a public API left open.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never worked with APIs what an API is, and why your company might open one to outside developers and charge for it. Name one limit or tradeoff of doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: An API is a published set of rules that tells outside software how to ask our system for something, such as a price estimate. The caller sends a request in an agreed format, with a key that identifies who is asking, and gets back structured data. We would open one to outside developers because partners can build on our service without us building every product ourselves, and we can charge per call or through paid tiers. The main tradeoff is that once customers depend on the API, we cannot change or retire it casually, and we have to run keys, quotas and rate limits so that one heavy client does not slow service for everyone else. Revenue has to justify that ongoing support cost.
rubricPoints: Defines an API as a published set of rules for requests and responses, not the provider's internal code
Explains the business case: partner reach, new channels and revenue from paid access
Names a real limit or tradeoff such as versioning commitments, support cost or capacity risk
Mentions keys, quotas or rate limits as the controls that make public access safe

suggested.rationale: Explaining the API idea and its business tradeoff back in plain words is the core skill here, and no listed mission teaches it directly.

lessons.plain: An API is a set of rules that lets one piece of software ask another for data or an action, such as a shop app asking a payment service to take a card payment. Once a company runs many of these APIs, the hard part is running them safely: deciding who may call them, how often, which version they use, and what each call is worth. API management is the layer that handles those jobs in one place, in front of the real services. Apigee is Google Cloud's product for this. The business case is that it lets a company open its services to partners or customers, watch usage, protect back-end systems from overload and abuse, and in some cases charge for access, without rewriting each service.
lessons.guessPrompt: A logistics company has 40 internal services that a dozen partner companies now want to call directly. Without any shared layer in front of them, what do you think goes wrong first, and what single capability would most reduce that risk?
lessons.teach:
An API gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of backend services and handles each incoming request before it reaches them. API management is the wider practice around that gateway: publishing APIs as products, controlling who can call them, limiting how much they can be used, tracking usage, and managing versions over time. Apigee is Google Cloud's API management product, and its business case rests on a few plain ideas.

Why it works: without a shared layer, each team bolts its own security checks, logging and limits onto each service, so the rules drift apart and gaps appear. A managed layer applies one policy everywhere. Authentication, which means proving who is calling (usually with a key or token), is checked once at the edge. A quota caps how many calls a given partner may make in a day, and a rate limit caps calls per second, so one busy client cannot starve everyone else.

Worked example: a vehicle-data company exposes a status API to three partners. Step 1: a partner sends a request with its key. Step 2: the gateway checks that the key is valid and active. Step 3: it checks that the partner's daily quota has room. Step 4: it forwards the request to the real service and records the call for usage reports. Step 5: if the partner has used its plan, the gateway returns a clear 'quota exceeded' response instead of letting the back end overload. Finance can then bill each partner from the recorded usage.

Common mistake: treating API management as only a security add-on. Much of its value comes from visibility and revenue: knowing which API earns money, which partner drives the load, and which version is still in use before it is retired.

Consequence: if one partner's script loops and sends thousands of requests, a managed gateway throttles that one client, while a team without one may see the whole service slow down for every customer.

The business case, in short, is faster and safer partner access, consistent governance, and measurable usage that supports pricing decisions.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital-scheduling vendor exposes an appointment-lookup API to six clinic apps on a Basic plan allowing 500 calls per day and 5 calls per second. Step 1: a clinic app sends a request with its key. Step 2: the gateway confirms the key is valid and active. Step 3: the gateway checks whether that clinic has used less than 5 calls in the current second, and lets the request continue if so. Step 4: [missing step]. Step 5: the request reaches the scheduling service and the call is recorded for usage reports.
choices: The gateway deletes the oldest usage records so the log stays under a size limit.
The gateway raises the clinic's daily quota automatically so the request can always succeed.
The gateway asks the scheduling service to re-verify the clinic's identity before forwarding anything.
The gateway checks whether the clinic's 500-call daily quota still has room, and returns a quota-exceeded response if it does not.
questions.why: The daily quota is a separate control from the per-second rate limit, and it is checked before the request is forwarded, so the missing step is the quota check that returns a clear quota-exceeded response when the daily cap is used up.

questions.prompt: A weather-data firm gives one partner a monthly allowance of 10,000 calls. That partner's script suddenly sends 20 calls within a single second, but its month-to-date total is still low. Which control is designed to stop this burst?
choices: A rate limit, which caps how many calls a client may make per second.
Authentication, which checks the identity of the partner by its key or token.
Version retirement, which removes an older API version from the gateway.
A quota, which caps how many calls a client may make per day or month.
questions.why: A rate limit caps calls per second, so it catches a short burst even when the longer-period total is still within allowance, while a quota counts over a longer period and would not stop this burst.

questions.prompt: A logistics company uses its API gateway only to check passwords and keys, and never reviews the usage records it produces. Which cost is the company most likely to miss as a result?
choices: The gateway refusing to forward any requests at all.
Not knowing which API version a partner still uses before retiring that version, or which partner drives the most load.
Slower authentication decisions at the edge of the network.
Failed key checks being shown to the wrong partner.
questions.why: Much of a managed gateway's value comes from the visibility and revenue data in its usage records, so ignoring those records hides which partners, versions and products matter for planning and pricing.

questions.prompt: A video-captioning company runs its API behind a managed gateway. One customer's batch job starts sending thousands of requests per minute. What is the most likely result?
choices: The gateway forwards every request, and all customers see the same slowdown.
The gateway throttles that one client's calls while other customers continue to get normal responses.
The gateway shuts down the entire API until the batch job finishes.
The gateway automatically moves the batch job's requests to a different company's API.
questions.why: A managed gateway applies per-client limits, so it slows or rejects only the misbehaving client, which protects the service for everyone else.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who runs our back-end services why the company would put Apigee in front of them, and name one real limit or tradeoff of adding this layer.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would say Apigee is a shared front door for our APIs. Instead of each service handling its own partner keys, limits and logging, the gateway checks those once, consistently, and forwards only valid traffic. The business case has three parts. Partners can be onboarded faster because access is self-service through a developer portal. We can see exactly which API and which partner drives load, which supports charging by usage or by plan. And our back ends are protected from one noisy client. The tradeoff is that it becomes one more component on every request path. It adds some latency and cost, needs its own configuration and an owner, and if it is misconfigured it can block legitimate traffic. So the case is strongest when we have many APIs or external consumers, and weaker for a single internal service with a few callers.
rubricPoints: Describes Apigee as an API management layer in front of backend services, not as the services themselves.
Names business benefits such as consistent security and governance, faster partner onboarding, and usage visibility.
Connects usage data to monetization or pricing decisions where relevant.
States a real tradeoff: an extra component that adds latency, cost and configuration ownership.
Explains when the case is strong, such as many APIs or many external consumers.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is stating the business case in your own words and naming its tradeoff, which no listed mission exercises directly.

lessons.plain: Cyber threats are the ways people or programs try to harm a computer system, steal from it, or stop it from working. Some flood a service with traffic until it cannot answer. Some lock a company's files and demand payment. Some trick a person into handing over a password. Some are simple mistakes, such as a storage area left open to anyone on the internet. Knowing the common types, and what each one costs a business in money, customer trust, or downtime, helps you spot which threats matter for a given system and who is responsible for guarding against each. It is a bit like knowing the ways a building can be broken into, flooded, or set on fire before you decide where the locks and sprinklers go.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine a company's online store goes down because thousands of fake visitors hit it every second, so real customers cannot load pages. Setting aside the technical name for this, what kind of harm is it, and what does the business lose? Try a sentence or two before reading on.
lessons.teach:
Each threat below is a type of harm, and each one hurts a business through money, customer trust, data, or uptime (the share of time a service is working). A DDoS (distributed denial of service) attack sends so much traffic from many sources that a service cannot answer real users. Ransomware is software that encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the key to unlock them. Malware is the general name for any malicious program, and ransomware and cryptomining are both kinds of it. Cryptomining secretly uses someone else's computing power to produce digital currency. Phishing is a deceptive message that tricks a person into giving away login details. Misconfiguration means a setting left wrong, such as a cloud storage area readable by anyone, and it is one of the most common causes of cloud data exposure. Unsecured third-party systems are vendors or partners with weak protections who connect to your environment. Physical damage covers fire, flood, or theft at the place where equipment sits. LLM attacks, such as prompt injection, trick a large language model (an AI system that generates text) into ignoring its rules or revealing data it should protect.

The business impact is what you should name when you classify a threat. DDoS causes lost sales and outages. Ransomware causes downtime and extortion. Cryptomining wastes compute and inflates the bill. Phishing and misconfiguration often lead to data breaches.

Worked example: an employee receives an email that looks like it comes from the payroll provider. It asks them to sign in again. Step one, the lure arrives. Step two, the employee types their password into a fake page. Step three, the attacker signs in with those valid credentials. Step four, the attacker copies customer records. Step five, the company must report the breach, which brings fines and lost trust. No computer was infected, yet the damage is real.

Common mistake: treating every threat as an outside attack. Misconfiguration is usually a setting the customer chose, not something a hacker did from afar.

Consequence: a cloud storage area left readable by anyone can be downloaded by strangers within minutes of the setting changing.

questions.prompt: A small design agency's cloud bill jumps overnight. Step one: a developer's access key is found in a public code repository. Step two: an outsider uses that key to start 30 large virtual machines in a region the agency never uses. Step three: those machines run software that secretly produces digital currency for the outsider. Step four is missing from this chain. Which option is the missing step, the one that shows the agency's business impact?
choices: Customers cannot reach the agency's website because traffic floods it, and sales drop.
The agency is billed for all the compute those machines used, so its bill is inflated by spending it never approved.
The attacker encrypts the agency's storage and demands payment for the key to unlock it.
The attacker copies customer records, and the agency must report a breach to regulators.
questions.why: Cryptomining wastes compute, and the impact named for it is an inflated bill, which is what step four must show.

questions.prompt: A partner company with weak security protections has a live connection into your network, and an attacker enters your environment through that partner. Which threat category does this describe?
choices: Distributed denial of service
Malware
Unsecured third-party systems
Physical damage
questions.why: Vendors or partners with weak protections that connect to your environment are the defining feature of unsecured third-party systems.

questions.prompt: An engineer switches a cloud storage area to readable by anyone for a quick test and forgets to switch it back. Which threat is this, and what business impact does it most often lead to?
choices: Malware, which mainly drains uptime
Misconfiguration, which often leads to a data breach
DDoS, which mainly causes lost sales
Ransomware, which mainly causes extortion by encryption
questions.why: A setting left wrong by the customer is a misconfiguration, and misconfiguration and phishing often lead to data breaches.

questions.prompt: A customer-support chatbot built on a large language model is sent a message containing hidden instructions that tell it to ignore its rules and reveal internal pricing rules. Which threat is this?
choices: Phishing, because a user is asked to give up a password
An LLM attack, specifically prompt injection
Ransomware, because the chatbot's data is locked
Cryptomining, because the chatbot uses extra computing power
questions.why: Prompt injection is an LLM attack that tricks a language model into ignoring its rules or revealing data it should protect.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that because our cloud provider runs strong data centers, we are safe from ransomware and phishing. In your own words, explain to them which parts of these threats the provider's protections help with, which parts stay mostly with us, and one limit of what you are saying.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them the provider protects the physical buildings, the hardware, and much of the underlying platform, so a thief cannot walk into a data center and a flood in one site should not take everything down. That helps against physical damage and some infrastructure attacks. It does not stop phishing, because a phishing email works on a person and gets that person's password, and the attacker then logs in as a real user. Ransomware can still arrive through a laptop or a misconfigured service we run. Our own settings, access rules, and staff habits stay mostly our responsibility. The limit of what I am saying is that provider protections reduce risk but do not remove it. The customer still has to configure services safely and train people to spot lures.
rubricPoints: Provider protections cover physical facilities and underlying infrastructure
Phishing and misconfiguration mostly depend on the customer's people and settings
Ransomware can reach customer systems through laptops or misconfigured services
Protections reduce risk but do not eliminate it

suggested.rationale: Classifying a described threat by type, business impact, and who guards against it is an exam-style reasoning skill that situations practice better than listing facts.

lessons.plain: Running your own servers in a room you control means you guard the building, the hardware, the network and the software yourself. Using a cloud provider changes who does which part of that job. The provider looks after the physical buildings, the servers and the core network. You still decide who can log in, which settings you switch on, and what data you store and who can see it. Cloud security is therefore less about walls around one building and more about who is allowed to do what, and about getting your own settings right. Knowing where the line sits is the first step to any cloud security decision.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company moves its customer database from servers in its own office to a cloud provider's data center, which parts of keeping that database safe do you think stop being the company's job, and which parts stay with the company? Give your best guess before reading on.
lessons.teach:
The shared responsibility model is the idea that security work is split between the cloud provider and the customer. The provider is responsible for security of the cloud: the physical data centers, the hardware, the underlying network, and the software that runs the platform itself. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: the data they store, the identities and access rules they set up, and the configuration of each service they switch on. The exact split moves with the service type. When you rent virtual machines, you manage more of the software stack yourself. With fully managed services, the provider takes on more of the software layers, but the customer still owns its data and who can access it.

On-premises security differs in several ways. In your own building you own every layer, so one team protects everything, usually behind a network boundary called a perimeter. In the cloud, resources are reachable across the internet and across many services, so identity (who or what is making a request) and configuration (how each setting is chosen) matter more than walls. Changes also happen fast. A new storage bucket can be created in seconds, so one wrong setting can expose data quickly.

Worked example: a company stores customer files in a cloud storage bucket. Step 1: the provider keeps the disks and data centers physically safe, which is the provider's job. Step 2: the company decides whether the bucket is public or private, which is the customer's job. Step 3: the company decides who holds access and whether it controls the encryption keys. If an engineer accidentally makes the bucket public, the exposure is the customer's responsibility, even though the provider's infrastructure did nothing wrong.

Common mistake: assuming that because the provider is large and well run, the data is automatically safe. Good infrastructure does not fix a wrong setting in your own account.

In a running system, misconfiguration is a frequent cause of cloud data exposure, so the customer's access and configuration reviews are an ongoing control, not a one-time setup.

questions.prompt: A regional pharmacy chain moves its prescription records into a managed database service run by a cloud provider. Step 1: the provider keeps the data center buildings, servers, and power supply physically secure. Step 2: the provider patches the database software it runs on the chain's behalf. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the chain's team reviews its audit log each week and finds that a former pharmacist's login can still read the records. Which completion for Step 3 fits the split of responsibility?
choices: Nothing is needed, because managed services are secured entirely by the provider.
The chain asks the provider to delete all records to be safe.
The chain removes the former pharmacist's login from its access settings.
The provider must remove the former pharmacist's login, since it operates the database for the chain.
questions.why: Who holds access and which logins exist is the customer's responsibility even when the provider runs the underlying database software.

questions.prompt: A freight company asks which of the following is the provider's job under the shared responsibility model.
choices: Deciding which drivers may view shipment data
Keeping the data center hardware and cooling physically protected
Choosing whether a storage bucket is public or private
Writing the access rules for the company's warehouse app
questions.why: Physical protection of data centers and hardware is security of the cloud, which the provider handles.

questions.prompt: A university research group rents virtual machines and installs its own web application on them. A flaw in that application is exploited. Who is mainly responsible for fixing it?
choices: Nobody, because the provider's network blocks all attacks
Only the operating system vendor, because it wrote the underlying software
The provider, because it owns the physical servers
The university group, because it installed and configures the application on machines it rents
questions.why: With rented virtual machines the customer manages more of the software stack, so application flaws fall to the customer.

questions.prompt: A startup assumes that because its cloud provider is large and well run, its customer files are safe by default. A developer then creates a storage bucket with public read access. What best explains the exposure?
choices: The provider's physical security failed, so the provider must fix the bucket.
Public access is a normal default that the provider must turn off for every bucket.
Cloud buckets cannot be made public, so the setting must be a bug in the provider's software.
The startup's own setting exposed the data, and good provider infrastructure does not undo a wrong configuration.
questions.why: Configuration in the customer's own account is the customer's responsibility, regardless of how well the provider runs its infrastructure.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says moving to the cloud means the provider handles security now, so we can stop worrying about it. Explain to them, in your own words, how cloud security differs from on-premises security, and name one limit or tradeoff of the shared split that they should keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd tell them the provider takes over the physical side: the buildings, the servers, and the core network. That is real work we no longer do. But the split means we still own what goes in: our data, who gets access, and how each service is configured. On our own servers we controlled the whole stack behind a network edge. In the cloud, access comes from identities and settings rather than walls, and one mistaken setting can expose a new resource within seconds. The tradeoff is that we have more to get right ourselves, so we need regular access reviews, logs we can actually check, and a clear owner for each setting. Exactly where the line sits depends on the service type. A managed database moves more of the software layer to the provider, but our data and access rules stay ours.
rubricPoints: The cloud provider secures the physical facilities, hardware and core platform, while the customer secures its data, identities and configurations.
The split between provider and customer shifts depending on the service type, such as rented machines versus managed services.
On-premises security relies on owning the whole stack behind a network perimeter, while cloud security leans more on identity and configuration.
A customer misconfiguration remains the customer's responsibility even when the provider's infrastructure is sound.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is explaining where the provider-customer line sits and why, which is best practised by talking it through with a teammate.

lessons.plain: Cloud security is about keeping information and services safe. Five ideas help organize that work: control (deciding who may do what), compliance (meeting the rules and laws that apply to your data and proving it), confidentiality (only the right people can read the data), integrity (data stays accurate and unaltered), and availability (systems are reachable when people need them). Think of a bank: a vault lock limits who gets in, regulators require audits, account statements must not be changed by accident, and branches must be open during business hours. A cloud security model needs all five, because protecting one while neglecting another still leaves real harm.
lessons.guessPrompt: A hospital stores patient records in the cloud. Nobody reads the records, but a fault deletes some of them and an engineer silently edits a few entries. Which of the five ideas (control, compliance, confidentiality, integrity, availability) does each problem harm, and why might the second be the harder one to notice?
lessons.teach: Control is the ability to decide who may do what with a system or its data, and to make sure those decisions are enforced. Confidentiality means information is seen only by those allowed to see it. Integrity means data stays accurate, complete and unaltered unless an authorized change is made. Availability means systems and data are reachable when people need them. Compliance means meeting the external rules that apply to your data, such as legal or industry requirements, and being able to show evidence that you do. These five matter together because a security model is only as strong as its weakest part. Consider a delivery company storing dispatch records in the cloud. Control: only the operations team's accounts can change routes, and every change is logged. Confidentiality: customer addresses are encrypted and readable only by approved services. Integrity: a route record cannot be quietly edited, so the log matches what really happened. Availability: the dispatch screen stays up at peak hours, with a second copy ready if one location fails. Compliance: records are kept for the period a regulator requires, and the company can produce proof. Responsibility is shared. The cloud provider secures the physical data centers, hardware and core infrastructure. The customer decides who gets access, configures settings, chooses where data lives, and meets its own legal obligations. Provider audit reports help the customer show things about the provider's side, but they do not prove the customer's own configuration. A common mistake is assuming a secure provider means a secure system. A storage location set to public exposes data, which is a confidentiality failure, even though every server underneath is well protected. In a running system, one missing control can break several ideas at once: an overprivileged account that deletes records harms integrity and availability together.

questions.prompt: A regional veterinary practice keeps appointment bookings in a cloud database. Step 1: A staff account with delete rights removes the bookings table by mistake, and the front desk cannot take or view appointments for a full day. Step 2: This is an availability failure, because the system is not reachable when staff need it. Step 3: ____ Which sentence completes Step 3, naming who owns the fix?
choices: Ask the cloud provider to restore power in its data center, since the provider secures the physical infrastructure.
Restrict delete rights to the accounts that need them and keep tested backups, since access decisions and backup settings belong to the customer.
Note that the disks are encrypted, so only confidentiality is at risk and no fix is needed for availability.
Treat the event as a compliance matter only, because no client records were seen by outsiders.
questions.why: Deciding who gets access and configuring backups are customer responsibilities, so restricting delete rights and keeping restorable copies is the customer's fix.

questions.prompt: A small museum's online ticketing system records sales totals. A staff script silently changes several totals without any authorized change being approved or logged. Which of the five ideas is directly violated?
choices: Availability, because the ticketing system could not be reached during the change.
Compliance, because the museum failed to publish its totals to the public.
Integrity, because the data is no longer accurate and unaltered unless an authorized change was made.
Confidentiality, because the totals were visible to someone who should not see them.
questions.why: Integrity means data stays accurate and unaltered unless an authorized change is made, and silent unauthorized edits break exactly that.

questions.prompt: A hospital network stores medical imaging files in cloud storage, and one storage location has been set to public so anyone with the link can read the files. Who is responsible for changing this setting?
choices: Both parties equally, because responsibility is always split down the middle.
The customer, because it configures storage settings and decides who may read its data.
The cloud provider, because it is responsible for the cloud platform as a whole.
Nobody, since the provider's audit report covers the storage service and shows it is secure.
questions.why: The customer configures settings and decides access, so a public storage setting is the customer's responsibility even though the provider secures the underlying servers.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm must keep client tax records for seven years. When an auditor asks for proof that the records were kept as required, the firm cannot produce any evidence. Which of the five ideas has failed?
choices: Confidentiality, because the auditor was allowed to see information they should not have.
Availability, because the records could not be reached when the auditor asked.
Control, because the firm did not decide who may do what with the records.
Compliance, because the firm cannot show evidence that it met the external record-keeping rules.
questions.why: Compliance means meeting external rules and being able to show evidence of it, and the firm cannot provide that evidence.

lessons.explainPrompt: A new teammate asks why we bother with five separate ideas instead of just making the system secure. In your own words, explain why control, compliance, confidentiality, integrity and availability all matter to a cloud security model, and name one limit or tradeoff of focusing on only one of them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Secure is too vague to check or assign. Splitting it into five ideas gives us five questions we can test. Confidentiality asks who can read the data. Integrity asks whether data can be changed without us noticing. Availability asks whether people can reach the service when they need it. Control asks who is allowed to make decisions and changes. Compliance asks whether we can prove we meet the rules that apply to us. The tradeoff is that strengthening one can weaken another. Locking access down hard protects confidentiality, but it can block the on-call engineer during an outage and hurt availability. So we set each control on purpose and check it against the others, rather than assuming one good setting covers everything.
rubricPoints: Defines each of the five ideas in plain terms and keeps them distinct from one another.
Explains that strengthening one idea can weaken another, such as strict access blocking recovery during an outage.
Notes that compliance means meeting external rules and being able to show evidence.
Recognizes that the provider secures the infrastructure while the customer secures its own access and configuration.

suggested.rationale: The objective is about reasoning through why several security goals matter together, and explaining that tradeoff back is the core skill.

lessons.plain: Security has its own vocabulary, and the words are easy to mix up. Some describe rules about who may do what, like least privilege, which means giving people only the access their job needs. Others describe how a system is built, like zero-trust, where every request is checked rather than trusted because it comes from inside the network. Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the right key can read it, and decryption reverses that. This lesson gives you these words so you can tell what a threat or control is about and who is responsible for it.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a new employee needs to read one folder for their job, should they receive access to the whole company file server just in case, and what could go wrong if they do?
lessons.teach:
Each term below names one idea, and together they cover rules, designs, and data protection.

Least privilege means every user, program, or service gets only the permissions needed for its task, and nothing more. Privileged access is the elevated access that can change settings, delete data, or grant rights to others, such as an administrator account. Because privileged access is so powerful, it should be granted rarely, limited in time where possible, and logged.

Zero-trust architecture is a design in which no request is trusted just because it comes from inside the network. Each request is checked for identity and permission. Security by default means a new system starts in its safest reasonable configuration, so an unsafe setting requires a deliberate choice. Security posture is the overall picture of how well protected an environment is at a given time, including misconfigurations and open exposures.

A firewall is a filter that allows or blocks network traffic based on rules about source, destination and port. Encryption converts readable data into scrambled data using a key; decryption reverses it with the correct key. Data loss prevention, usually shortened to DLP, is tooling that finds sensitive data such as card numbers and blocks or flags its movement. Cyber resilience is the ability to keep operating, recover, and return to normal after an attack or failure, not only to prevent it.

Worked example: a support script needs to read customer records from one database table. Under least privilege, you create an account with read access to that table only. If the account's key is stolen, the attacker can read one table, not the whole database. Had the account been an administrator, the damage would be far larger.

Common mistake: treating a firewall as enough. A firewall controls the path, but if an allowed port hosts a vulnerable app or a storage bucket is public, the firewall does nothing about it.

In a running system, a leaked administrator key with no least-privilege limits can delete production data within minutes, which is why both access limits and tested backups matter.

questions.prompt: A clinic's billing app stores every patient invoice in encrypted form, so the stored files look like scrambled data. Here are the steps: (1) The app takes the readable invoice text and encrypts it using key K. (2) Only the scrambled version is written to storage. (3) Missing step: when a billing clerk who holds key K opens an invoice, the application ___. Complete the missing step.
choices: deletes the scrambled copy so only a readable copy remains
encrypts the scrambled data again with a second key so it is harder to read
uses key K to decrypt the stored data back into readable text for the clerk
converts the invoice into a one-way hash that cannot be reversed
questions.why: Decryption is the reverse of encryption and needs the correct key, so using key K to turn the stored scrambled data back into readable text is the missing step.

questions.prompt: A contractor needs to read the log files in one storage bucket for one week to diagnose a fault. Which access setup best applies least privilege?
choices: An administrator account for the whole project, so the contractor is never blocked
A read-and-write account for every bucket in the project, to be safe
A read-only account limited to that one log bucket, removed after the week
A shared login used by the whole operations team, so no new account is needed
questions.why: Least privilege means granting only the permissions needed for the task, so a read-only account for one bucket that expires matches the job and nothing more.

questions.prompt: A company's firewall allows only web traffic into its network, but one of its storage buckets has been set to public, so anyone on the internet can list its files. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The firewall is the only control that matters, so the bucket is safe while the firewall is on
This is a cyber resilience failure, because the firewall stopped the files from being recovered
The firewall does not govern the bucket, so the open exposure is a posture issue to fix directly
The firewall covers the bucket too, so the public setting has no real effect
questions.why: A firewall filters network paths but does not control what a public storage resource exposes, so the open setting is a security posture problem that needs its own correction.

questions.prompt: A shipping company is hit by an attack that encrypts its files and demands payment. Within a few hours it rebuilds its systems from backups it had tested and returns to normal operations. Which term best describes that ability?
choices: Encryption
Least privilege
Cyber resilience
Security by default
questions.why: Cyber resilience is the ability to keep operating, recover, and return to normal after an attack, which is what the company did, rather than preventing the attack.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says 'we have a firewall, so our data is secure.' In your own words, explain to them what a firewall does, what it does not cover, and which two other terms from this lesson would close the gap, naming one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: A firewall filters network traffic by rules about where it comes from, where it goes, and which port it uses. It decides what can reach a system, but it does not check whether the service behind it is configured or patched safely. If an allowed port runs a vulnerable application, or a storage bucket is set to public, the firewall still lets the traffic through. Two other ideas help close that gap. Least privilege limits what any account can do even after an attacker gets in, though tight permissions add administrative work and need regular review. Encryption protects data at rest and in transit, so stolen copies are unreadable without the key, but it does not stop someone with valid access from reading data they are allowed to see, and the keys themselves must be guarded. Together these are layers, not a single guarantee.
rubricPoints: A firewall filters traffic by source, destination and port rules.
A firewall does not check whether an allowed service is configured or patched safely.
Least privilege limits damage from a compromised account, at the cost of extra administration.
Encryption protects stolen or intercepted data, but only while the keys stay protected.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is telling these terms apart and explaining them to someone else, which an explanation exercise tests better than a hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles data so that only someone holding the right key can read it. Data can be in three states: sitting in storage (at rest), moving across a network (in transit), or being actively processed in memory (in use). Each state faces different threats, so protection is applied to each one. Think of a letter: it is locked in a box at the warehouse, carried in a sealed van, and opened only by the recipient who holds the key. Knowing which state you are protecting tells you which control to reach for.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company encrypts its database files on disk. Is a copy of those files that gets stolen from a backup tape still readable, and what might still be exposed while the application is running?
lessons.teach:
Encryption turns readable data, called plaintext, into scrambled data, called ciphertext, using a key. Decryption reverses this using the correct key. Protection depends on where the data is, so think in three usage states. At rest means data sitting in storage such as disks, databases and backups. In transit means data moving between two points, such as a phone talking to a server or one service calling another over a network. In use means data being actively processed in a program's memory.

Why it works: someone who copies scrambled bytes without the key learns nothing useful, so the key is what must be guarded. Storage encryption protects against stolen disks and leaked backups. Transit encryption, usually TLS (Transport Layer Security, the protocol behind HTTPS), protects against anyone who can observe the network path. In-use protection, such as Confidential Computing, uses hardware that keeps memory encrypted and isolated while work runs, so even the host operating system should not see plain data.

Worked example: a driver app sends a position update to an API over HTTPS, which is in transit. The API writes the update to a managed database whose storage is encrypted, which is at rest. The API runs on a Confidential VM, a virtual machine whose memory is protected, which is in use. Each hop needs its own control; the first does not cover the second.

Common mistake: assuming that because the disk is encrypted, the data is safe everywhere. If the API calls a backend over plain HTTP inside the network, anyone who can observe that traffic reads every position in transit, even though the database is encrypted.

Consequence: in a running dispatch system, a missing transit control lets anyone on the path read positions and driver identifiers, and an encrypted database offers no protection against that.

The cloud provider encrypts data at rest by default and encrypts much traffic inside its own network. The customer chooses keys, decides whether to manage them, enforces TLS in its own applications, and decides whether to use in-use protections. Each state needs a deliberate control.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company's unlock flow is traced in three hops. Hop 1: a rider's phone sends the unlock request to the company's API over HTTPS, which encrypts the connection between the phone and the server. This is the in-transit state. Hop 2: the API writes the trip record to a database whose disks are encrypted, which is the at-rest state. Hop 3 is missing: a fleet analytics dashboard server pulls trip records from the database across the company's internal network, using plain unencrypted connections. Which usage state does Hop 3 describe, and what control covers it?
choices: In use; a Confidential VM that keeps the dashboard's memory encrypted
In transit; the database's disk encryption, which also protects the network path
At rest; disk encryption on the dashboard server's storage
In transit; TLS on the internal connection between the database and the dashboard server
questions.why: Hop 3 moves data between two points over a network, so it is in transit, and only transport encryption such as TLS protects it, because disk encryption does nothing for data on the wire.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility's field gateway uploads pump pressure readings to a cloud service over TLS, and the cloud service then stores the readings on encrypted disks. Which usage state does the gateway-to-cloud upload describe?
choices: Plaintext
At rest
In use
In transit
questions.why: Data moving between two points over a network is in transit, and TLS is the protection for that state, while encrypted disks cover the later storage step.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs its rate-quote service on a Confidential VM, whose memory stays encrypted while work runs. The quote service calls a separate pricing service over plain HTTP on the internal network. The firm says all of its data is protected because the Confidential VM is encrypted. What is the accurate assessment?
choices: Not protected in transit, because the pricing calls cross the network unencrypted, even though the in-use memory is protected
Protected only if the pricing service's database also has encrypted disks
Protected: the Confidential VM covers every usage state, including network traffic
Not protected at all, because memory encryption only ever applies to data at rest
questions.why: The calls between the two services are in transit and need TLS, and in-use memory protection on the quote service does not cover data that travels over the network.

questions.prompt: A small clinic runs its own patient-booking web app on a cloud platform. The app still accepts some connections over plain HTTP. Who is responsible for turning on encryption for those connections?
choices: Google, because the cloud provider encrypts all traffic inside its network automatically
The clinic, because it must enforce TLS in its own application for the connections it controls
Neither party, because the platform's default storage encryption also covers the app's public connections
Google, because the cloud provider encrypts data at rest by default
questions.why: The provider encrypts storage by default and much traffic inside its own network, but the customer is responsible for enforcing TLS in the applications it builds and runs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud security how encryption at rest, in transit, and in use differ, and name one limit of encryption that a team still has to handle with other controls.
lessons.modelAnswer: Encryption at rest protects stored data, such as disks, databases and backups, so a stolen disk is unreadable without the key. Encryption in transit protects data moving across a network, usually with TLS, so someone watching the wire sees only scrambled bytes. Encryption in use protects data while a program is processing it, using hardware-protected memory such as Confidential Computing. These are separate controls, and turning on one does not cover the others. One limit to remember is that encryption does not stop someone who has legitimate access to the running system. If an application or an administrator has the key and the permission to read, the data is decrypted for them. So a team still needs access control, least privilege and logging alongside encryption.
rubricPoints: Defines at rest, in transit and in use with a clear example of each
Explains that each state needs its own control and one does not cover the others
Names a limit, such as authorized users or apps still seeing decrypted data
Notes that access control and logging must complement encryption

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a described situation about which state is exposed and which control fits adds more than reading a list of facts.

lessons.plain: Three different questions get asked whenever someone uses a system. Authentication asks who you are, and it is answered by proving it, for example with a password plus a code from your phone. Authorization asks what you are allowed to do once the system knows who you are. Auditing asks what happened, by keeping a record of who did what so it can be reviewed later. A building badge makes a useful comparison: the reader checks the badge is genuine, the door lock decides which rooms you may enter, and the security log notes when you went in.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new contractor signs in to your company's cloud console with the correct password, then tries to delete a database they were never meant to touch and is refused. Which idea refused the deletion, and which idea would let you find out later that the attempt happened?
lessons.teach:
Authentication is the act of proving an identity. A user types a password, approves a prompt on a phone, or taps a security key. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) means requiring two or more different kinds of proof, such as something you know (a password) and something you have (a phone or hardware key). Google calls its version 2-Step Verification (2SV). Authentication answers only the question of who is connecting.

Authorization is the decision about what that identity may do. In Google Cloud this is handled by Identity and Access Management (IAM). IAM grants roles to principals (users, groups, or service accounts) on resources such as a project or a storage bucket. A role is a named bundle of permissions. Following least privilege, you give each principal only the roles its work needs. Authorization is checked on every request, after authentication has succeeded.

Auditing is the record of what happened. Cloud Audit Logs, read through Cloud Logging, capture administrative changes such as a role being granted, and data access events where they are enabled. Auditing prevents nothing by itself; it lets people review activity and investigate afterwards.

Worked example: Priya signs in with her password and a code from her phone, so authentication succeeds. She then asks to delete a production bucket. IAM checks her roles on that bucket, finds only a viewer role, and refuses the request, which is authorization. Both the successful sign-in and the refused delete are written to the audit logs, which is auditing.

Common mistake: treating a successful login as permission to do anything. Passing authentication does not imply authorization, and a logged event is not the same as a blocked one.

Consequence in a running system: if an attacker steals a password from an account without MFA, they pass authentication and inherit every role that account holds. Broad roles combined with thin logging make the damage large and slow to trace.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental's contractor Rafael signs in with his password and a six-digit code from his authenticator app, so authentication succeeds. He then asks to read a billing export in a finance dataset. IAM checks his roles on that dataset, finds a Dataset Viewer role that includes reading, and allows the read. Step 3 is missing: what happens in the audit record of that read?
choices: Nothing is written, because reads of stored data are never captured by Google Cloud audit logging.
The read is recorded only if data access logging is enabled for that dataset, and then it is kept for later review.
The logging system checks the read again after the fact and reverses it if the role was not meant to allow it.
The read is written to the audit logs as a denied event, because it was a sensitive dataset and the request is recorded as blocked.
questions.why: Audit logs capture data access events only where that logging is switched on, and when it is on the allowed read is recorded for later review, not blocked.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's engineer taps a hardware security key and then enters a PIN. Which statement best describes what this sign-in step establishes?
choices: It proves the engineer is who they claim to be, but says nothing about what the engineer is allowed to change.
It creates a permanent log of every change the engineer makes for later review by the security team.
It decides which storage buckets the engineer may delete, based on the roles assigned to the engineer.
It removes any roles the engineer does not need, which is the purpose of applying least privilege.
questions.why: Using a key plus a PIN is authentication, which only establishes identity; permissions (authorization) and records (auditing) are separate controls.

questions.prompt: A small agency's contractor has a password stolen through a phishing email. The account has no second factor enabled and holds Project Editor on three projects. The attacker signs in successfully. Which control gap most directly let the attacker get past the first gate?
choices: The Project Editor role was broader than least privilege requires, so the attacker could make changes after signing in.
IAM was not checking roles on the three projects at all, so every request was allowed without review.
Audit logging was switched off, so the sign-in could not be recorded and the attacker went unnoticed.
There was no second factor such as 2SV, so a stolen password alone was enough to pass authentication.
questions.why: The first gate is authentication, and without a second factor a stolen password alone passes it; the broad role matters after that gate, not at it.

questions.prompt: A city council's IT lead needs to find out who changed a firewall rule on a shared project last Tuesday. Which Google Cloud capability answers this question?
choices: 2-Step Verification, which confirms the identity of whoever signed in to the project
Cloud Audit Logs read through Cloud Logging, which record administrative changes such as the rule edit
A least privilege review, which lists the roles each group holds on the project
IAM role checks, which decide in advance what each principal is permitted to do
questions.why: Administrative changes are recorded by Cloud Audit Logs, which is the auditing function, while the other three handle authentication or authorization and do not produce a history of who changed what.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who says 'we have MFA, so we are secure' how authentication, authorization and auditing differ. Name one limit that MFA alone does not solve.
lessons.modelAnswer: MFA only strengthens authentication: it makes it harder to prove that a user is who they claim to be, by requiring a second kind of proof such as a phone approval. It does not decide what that user can do. Authorization is the separate step, handled by IAM, where roles granted to a principal on a resource determine which actions are allowed. Auditing is the third step, a record in Cloud Audit Logs of who signed in and what they changed or tried to change, which supports later review. The limit is that MFA cannot stop a legitimate user from holding excessive roles, and it cannot stop an attacker who completes the second factor, for example through a phished one-time code. Least privilege in IAM and regular log review cover what MFA leaves open.
rubricPoints: Authentication proves identity, and MFA or 2SV adds a second kind of proof.
Authorization decides allowed actions, and in Google Cloud this is IAM roles on resources.
Auditing records activity for later review and does not block anything.
MFA does not limit what a valid user can do, so least privilege and logging are still needed.

suggested.rationale: Telling apart three similar-sounding controls in a described situation is best practised by reasoning through short scenarios that mix sign-in, permission and record-keeping.

lessons.plain: Security posture is the overall picture of how well protected a company's systems are right now: which settings are safe, which doors are left open, and which fixes are missing. Threat intelligence is organised knowledge about the attackers who might come after you: what they tend to do, which tools they use, and the telltale signs such as a suspicious internet address or a file fingerprint. Threat response is what a team does after something suspicious happens: stop the damage, remove the attacker, get services working again, and learn from it. Think of a house. The state of its locks and windows is the posture, news about burglars in your area is the intelligence, and what you do when the alarm sounds is the response.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company hears that a criminal group is attacking firms in its industry, but nothing has happened to it yet. What would you check first, and what would you prepare so you could act quickly if someone got in?
lessons.teach:
Security posture is a snapshot of how well an environment is defended at a given time. It covers configuration (is a storage area open to the public?), access (do administrators use multi-factor sign-in, a second check beyond a password?), patching (are known flaws fixed?) and logging (are records of activity being kept?). Posture changes every day as systems change, so it has to be re-checked continuously. In a cloud setting, much of it depends on how the customer configures their own resources.

Threat intelligence is evidence-based knowledge about attackers: who they are, what they target, which techniques they use, and the indicators that reveal them, such as a malicious address, a domain name or a file hash, which is a fingerprint of a file's contents. Intelligence is only useful with context. An indicator on its own tells you little; one tied to a known campaign tells you what to check next.

Threat response is the set of actions taken once a threat is suspected or confirmed. The usual order is to contain (stop the spread, for example by disabling a compromised account), eradicate (remove the attacker's foothold), recover (restore trusted services) and learn (close the gap that allowed it and update posture).

Worked example. Intelligence reports that a group guesses passwords from a particular address range against firms like yours. A posture review shows one administrator account lacks multi-factor sign-in. Step 1: you block the range and enforce multi-factor sign-in on that account. Step 2: logs later show successful sign-ins from the range anyway, so the account must have been compromised. Step 3, response: contain by revoking its sessions and resetting its credentials, eradicate by checking for accounts or scheduled tasks the attacker created, recover by confirming normal access, and learn by asking why that account was exempt.

Common mistake: treating posture as a one-time audit, or blocking intelligence indicators without checking whether they still matter.

A slow response lets an attacker keep moving through a running system, so containment comes before a full investigation.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic's file server shows that a file hash matches one tied to a known ransomware campaign, which encrypts shared folders and demands payment. A search finds the same hash on one reception workstation. Step 1: the team confirms the match and treats the threat as confirmed. Step 2, contain: they disconnect that workstation from the network so the malware cannot reach the shared folders. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, recover: they restore the shared folders from a backup that was checked as clean. Which action belongs in the missing Step 3, which comes between containment and recovery?
choices: Schedule a review of the clinic's password policy for next quarter
Write a lessons-learned note about how the malware reached the reception desk
Remove the malware and any scheduled task or startup entry it created on the workstation
Add the file hash to the firewall block list and leave the workstation connected
questions.why: Eradicate means removing the attacker's foothold, such as the malware and anything it set up to persist, before trusted services are restored.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's posture snapshot shows two gaps: one cloud storage bucket is open to the public with no activity logging turned on, and a threat feed lists a malicious domain name that has not been seen in the firm's logs for two years. Which finding is a posture gap rather than a threat indicator?
choices: The public storage bucket with logging turned off
The feed's report that the domain was once used by a campaign
The absence of any recent logins from the domain
The malicious domain name listed in the feed
questions.why: Posture describes how the environment is configured and defended right now, so a publicly open bucket without logs is a configuration and logging gap, while the domain is an indicator from intelligence.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm blocked an address that threat intelligence linked to a password-guessing group. The team then marked the risk as closed and did not check anything else. What is the main mistake in this approach?
choices: The team should have deleted all logs from the period when the address was active
The team should have waited for the attacker to attempt a second login before acting
Blocking an address is never a valid control, so it should not have been used
The team did not check whether the indicator was still relevant or whether the account posture gaps were fixed
questions.why: Intelligence indicators need context and currency, and posture is a continuing snapshot, so closing the risk after one block misses both checks the course describes.

questions.prompt: An online retailer discovers that an API key for its payment service has been used from an unfamiliar address in another country. The security lead is considering what to do first. Which action best fits the order of threat response described in the course?
choices: Rotate all keys on the normal annual schedule next year
Write a full forensic report before touching the key, so the findings are complete
Delete the access logs for the affected week to save storage space
Disable the compromised key and end its active sessions to stop the spread, then investigate
questions.why: Containment comes first to stop an attacker moving through a running system, so disabling the key and its sessions precedes the wider investigation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to security the difference between security posture, threat intelligence and threat response. For each one, name a limit or tradeoff it carries.
lessons.modelAnswer: Security posture is a snapshot of how well our systems are defended right now: settings, access rules, patches and logging. Its limit is that it goes stale as soon as something changes, so it needs repeated checks rather than one audit. Threat intelligence is knowledge about attackers, such as their techniques and the indicators they leave behind. Its limit is that indicators age quickly; an address that was malicious last month may be harmless now, so we weigh them against context rather than blocking blindly. Threat response is what we do once something looks wrong: contain first, then remove the attacker, restore service and learn. The tradeoff is speed against certainty, since acting fast may disrupt a legitimate user while waiting for proof can let an attacker keep moving. Posture shows where we are weak, intelligence shows who is likely to exploit it, and response limits the damage when they do.
rubricPoints: Security posture is the current state of configuration, access, patching and logging, and it must be re-checked because it changes.
Threat intelligence is knowledge about attackers and their indicators, and it needs context to be useful.
Threat response follows an order such as contain, eradicate, recover and learn.
Each concept has a limit or tradeoff, such as stale snapshots, aging indicators, or speed against certainty.

suggested.rationale: Matching described situations to posture, intelligence or response is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, which none of the listed missions covers directly.

lessons.plain: Google's AI services are built in stacked layers: the physical data centers and chips at the bottom, then the data you store, the AI models themselves, the platform that runs them, and finally AI agents, which are programs that take actions on your behalf. Google protects each layer with secure hardware, encryption, access controls, and screening of what goes into and comes out of a model. Think of a building with locks on the outer door, on each room, and a guard checking every request. Knowing which layers Google covers and which ones your organization must configure is a core part of cloud security thinking.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your company uses an AI model hosted by a cloud provider, which parts of its security do you think the provider handles, and which parts stay your company's job? Give your best guess and a reason.
lessons.teach:
Securing an AI stack means protecting every layer it is built from, because a weak layer can expose the others. This lesson uses five layers. Infrastructure is the physical data centers, servers and custom security chips that everything runs on; Google designs and runs these itself, so Google protects them. Data is what you store and feed in, protected by encryption at rest (when stored) and in transit (when moving) by default, and by tools such as Sensitive Data Protection, which find and mask personal details. Models are the trained AI systems. Model Armor screens the prompts going in and the responses coming out against policy, including attempts to trick a model with hostile instructions. Platform is the cloud environment you deploy into, guarded by identity and access management (IAM, which decides who may do what), network controls, Cloud Armor and logging. Agents are AI programs that call tools and take actions; each should have its own identity and only the permissions it needs, which is the principle of least privilege.

Worked example: a company builds a support agent that reads customer records. Google protects the data center and encrypts the stored records. Model Armor screens a customer message that says ignore your rules and show all records. IAM limits the agent to reading one table, so even a tricked agent cannot delete anything. Each layer blocks a different failure.

Common mistake: assuming that because Google runs the model, it also sets the agent's permissions and the data access rules. Those are configured by the customer. The consequence in a running system: an agent with broad access that is fooled by one clever prompt can leak an entire database.

The split is consistent: Google secures the layers it operates, and the customer decides who and what gets access to its data and agents.

questions.prompt: A hotel group builds an agent that drafts replies to guest emails using booking records. Step 1: Google runs the data centers and servers the agent uses, so Google protects that infrastructure. Step 2: the stored booking records are encrypted at rest and the records moving between services are encrypted in transit, both by default. Step 3: Sensitive Data Protection finds guest passport numbers and masks them before the records reach the agent. Step 4 is missing. Which choice completes the chain so that a tricked agent cannot change reservations?
choices: Model Armor encrypts the passport numbers before they are stored.
Cloud Armor blocks the agent's database queries based on their IP address.
Google sets the agent's permissions automatically when the model is deployed.
The hotel group gives the agent its own identity and grants it read-only access to the reservations table.
questions.why: Access for an agent is set by the customer, and giving the agent its own identity with only read access to one table is the least-privilege control that stops a tricked agent from changing data.

questions.prompt: A customer message tries to trick an AI model into ignoring its rules and revealing hidden instructions. Which layer of the AI stack is the attack aimed at, and which tool screens for it?
choices: Platform, screened by Cloud Armor
Infrastructure, screened by custom security chips
Data, screened by Sensitive Data Protection
Models, screened by Model Armor
questions.why: Hostile instructions aimed at a trained model belong to the models layer, and Model Armor is the tool that screens prompts and responses against policy.

questions.prompt: A new support agent was given a service account with broad rights across the whole project, so one tricked prompt let it delete storage buckets it had no reason to touch. Which principle was broken?
choices: Data masking
Least privilege
Network segmentation
Encryption in transit
questions.why: Least privilege means an agent gets only the permissions it needs, and this agent had far more than a support task required.

questions.prompt: A retailer asks who must decide which employees and agents may open its customer records. Which answer is right?
