Reliability is the ability of a system to do its intended job correctly and consistently over time, including after something breaks. A reliable system is one users can depend on. Reliability is broader than uptime alone, because a service that is up but returns wrong answers is not reliable.

High availability (often shortened to HA) is a design property: the service stays accessible even when one of its components fails. The usual way to get it is redundancy, meaning more than one copy of each critical part, plus a way to send traffic only to healthy copies. Availability is usually expressed as the share of time the service is up.

Worked example. A positions API runs on one virtual machine. At 02:00 its disk fails and the API is down for 40 minutes until an engineer rebuilds it. Now run two machines in different zones (separate data centers within one region) behind a load balancer, which spreads requests across machines. A health check, a periodic test asking each machine whether it responds, runs continuously. Step 1: machine A fails. Step 2: the health check stops getting answers from A. Step 3: the load balancer stops sending it traffic. Step 4: machine B serves every request. Users may see a few failed requests during detection, but the service stays up.

Common mistake: assuming high availability means nothing ever fails. Failure is expected; HA limits how far a failure spreads. Placing both machines in the same zone weakens protection, since one zone outage takes out both.

In a running system, a single point of failure is any part whose loss stops the whole service. Finding those is usually the first step toward reliability.

questions.prompt: A ticket-tracking app runs three web servers in one region, each in a different zone, behind a load balancer that spreads requests across them. A health check tests each server every 10 seconds. Here is what happens during a zone outage. Step 1: the zone hosting server 2 loses power, so server 2 stops responding. Step 2: the health check gets no answer from server 2 and marks it unhealthy. Step 3 is left blank for you to fill in. Step 4: servers 1 and 3 handle all new requests, so the app stays up with a brief dip in requests during detection. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: An engineer rebuilds server 2 by hand before any traffic is moved
The load balancer stops sending new requests to server 2
The health check is switched off so that server 2 keeps its share of traffic
Users are told to retry their requests against server 2's address
questions.why: Once the health check marks server 2 unhealthy, the load balancer stops routing traffic to it, which is what lets the healthy servers take over.

questions.prompt: A shop's checkout page returns a success status on every request, but for some customers it shows the wrong total. Which statement best describes this system?
choices: It is reliable in terms of uptime but fails the operational excellence test because it has no dashboards
It is reliable, because reliability is measured only by the share of time the service is accessible
It is highly available, so the problem is only a reliability concern for the payment team
It is not reliable, because reliability means doing the intended job correctly and consistently, and wrong answers count as failures even when the page is up
questions.why: Reliability covers correct and consistent work over time, so a service that is up but returns wrong totals is not reliable.

questions.prompt: A regional file-storage service keeps its only storage cluster in one zone. A team wants the most direct change to raise its high availability. Which change does that?
choices: Schedule all software upgrades for weekends so fewer users notice problems
Double the CPU of the existing cluster so it recovers faster after a crash
Add a second copy of the storage cluster in a different zone and route traffic only to whichever copies pass their health checks
Keep nightly backups and restore them by hand after any outage
questions.why: High availability comes from redundancy across separate failure domains plus routing only to healthy copies, which a second zone copy with health-checked routing provides.

questions.prompt: A team says: our system is designed for high availability, so failures should not happen and we can skip monitoring and post-incident reviews. Which response is most accurate?
choices: The team is partly right about HA but wrong to skip operations, because HA limits how far a failure spreads while failures are still expected, so monitoring and learning from incidents remain necessary
The team should keep HA but move all operations work to the design phase so it is never needed in production
The team should drop HA and rely only on post-incident reviews, since monitoring adds cost without benefit
The team is right, because a high availability design removes the need for operations work
questions.why: High availability limits failure spread but does not prevent failures, so monitoring, incident response and learning from failures are still part of operational excellence.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between reliability and high availability, and name one limit of high availability.
lessons.modelAnswer: Reliability is about whether the system does its job correctly and consistently over time, including when parts fail. High availability is one way to get there: it means the service keeps answering even when a component dies, usually by running redundant copies behind a load balancer that stops sending traffic to any copy that fails its health check. So availability is one part of reliability, not the whole thing. The limit I'd flag is that high availability only covers the failures you designed for. Two servers in the same zone still go down together if that zone fails, and a service that stays up while returning wrong data is available but not reliable. Operational excellence sits above both: it is the monitoring, automation and post-incident learning that keep reliability from slipping over time.
rubricPoints: Reliability means doing the intended job correctly and consistently, not just being up.
High availability keeps a service reachable when a component fails, usually through redundancy and automatic traffic redirection.
Availability is one part of reliability; high availability is a design choice aimed at it.
Names a limit: HA covers designed-for failures, while correlated failures in one zone or wrong answers still cause harm.
Operational excellence is the ongoing practice of monitoring, automation and learning from incidents that sustains reliability.

suggested.rationale: Distinguishing these terms and naming their limits in your own words is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine targets this vocabulary directly.

lessons.plain: Designing for resilience means building a system so it keeps working, or recovers quickly, when parts of it fail. Think of a bakery with a spare oven, a second kitchen ready to take orders, and a recipe book stored in a fireproof safe. Redundancy means keeping spare parts or capacity. Replication means keeping copies of data in more than one place as it changes. Scalable infrastructure means resources that grow when demand rises and shrink when it falls. Backups are saved snapshots of data from a point in time, kept so you can rebuild after damage, mistakes or attacks. Each practice solves a different kind of failure, and a good design usually uses several together.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your online store runs on one server in one building. If that building loses power for six hours, what happens to customers, and what would you add to prevent or shorten that outage?
lessons.teach:
Resilience is a system's ability to keep serving users, or to recover, when something fails. Four practices do most of the work. Redundancy means running spare copies of a component, so losing one does not stop the service. Replication means copying data to another machine or location, usually continuously, so a second copy is ready. Scalable infrastructure means capacity that adds or removes resources automatically as demand changes, using rules such as average CPU use. A backup is a saved copy of data taken at a past point in time, kept separately so you can restore after deletion, corruption or attack.

Why it works: each practice covers a different failure. Redundancy and scaling handle hardware loss and traffic spikes. Replication shortens recovery when a whole site fails. Backups recover from logical damage, such as a bad delete, that copies faithfully spread.

Worked example: a ride-dispatch database runs in one zone, which is one isolated data center inside a region. Step 1: at 10:00 the zone loses power. With no replica, the service is down until someone rebuilds from the last nightly backup, and the morning's updates are lost. Step 2: with a replica in a second zone, the system promotes the replica and dispatchers resume within minutes, with only the last few seconds of writes at risk. Step 3: at 11:00 an engineer runs a script that deletes rows by mistake. The replica deletes them too, because it copies every change. Only a point-in-time backup from 10:59 can restore them.

Common mistake: treating replication as a backup. Replication protects against hardware and site failure; backups protect against mistakes and attacks.

Consequence: a system with replicas but no tested backups can lose data permanently in one bad command. Resilience is a set of practices that must be tested together, not a single setting.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs its patient-scheduling service on three identical web servers behind a load balancer, which spreads requests across them. Step 1: at 09:00 one server's disk fails. The other two keep answering requests, so patients notice nothing. Step 2: at 12:00 a flu-vaccine campaign triples traffic. The server group has a rule to add a server whenever average CPU use stays above 70 percent, so it adds servers until CPU drops. Step 3 is missing from this trace. At 15:00 a faulty update corrupts the appointment database on the live copy and on its replica in a second zone, because both copy every change. Step 4: the team restores the appointment database from a point-in-time backup taken at 14:59, before the update ran. Which practice is the missing step 3 illustrating, as the reason restoring from a backup is needed here?
choices: Replication, because a second zone holding the corrupt data proves the failover was successful
Scalable infrastructure, because adding servers at 12:00 made the database write more slowly
Redundancy, because the spare web servers should have kept a clean copy of the appointment data
Backups, because replication copies the corruption to the replica, so only a saved past copy can undo it
questions.why: Replication copies the damage as faithfully as it copies good data, so only a backup taken before the corruption can recover from logical damage like this.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines replication as the term is used in cloud resilience?
choices: Keeping a saved copy of data from a past moment, stored apart from the live system
Adding or removing compute capacity automatically as the amount of demand changes
Copying data to another machine or location, usually continuously, so a second copy is ready
Running extra identical components so that the loss of one does not stop the service
questions.why: Replication is the continuous copying of data to another machine or location so a second copy is ready, while the other options describe backups, redundancy, and scaling.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps its shipment-tracking database replicated to a second zone. An employee runs a bad command at 16:20 that deletes 2,000 shipment records. Which statement is correct?
choices: Replication makes backups unnecessary, because two copies of the data always exist
The replica still holds the deleted rows, so no restore is needed
The replica also deletes the rows, so a backup taken before 16:20 is needed to restore them
Autoscaling will recreate the deleted rows on new servers within minutes
questions.why: A replica copies every change including deletes, so only a backup from before the mistake can restore the records.

questions.prompt: A small online bookshop wants its storefront to keep working if one server fails and to absorb a sudden surge in traffic without an engineer making manual changes. Which combination of practices addresses both needs?
choices: Redundant spare servers plus automatic scaling based on a rule such as average CPU use
One very large server with a replicated copy of its database
Nightly backups plus a scheduled restore job each morning
Manual restarts of the web server every hour during busy periods
questions.why: Redundancy covers losing a server and automatic scaling covers traffic spikes, which are the two failures this bookshop needs handled without manual intervention.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between replication and backups. Name one limit of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: A replica is a continuously updated copy of a database or storage bucket in another location. If the main site fails, I can switch to the copy and keep running with little data loss, so replication is mainly about availability. Its limit is that it copies mistakes too. If someone deletes the wrong rows, the replica deletes them as well. So I would also keep point-in-time backups in a separate place. A backup can restore the data as it was at an earlier time, but bringing it back into service takes longer than a failover. Replication keeps us up; backups let us go back in time. We need both, plus regular restore tests to prove the backups actually work.
rubricPoints: Replication keeps a continuously updated copy in another location, enabling fast failover.
Replication copies mistakes and corruption too, so it is not a backup.
Backups are point-in-time copies kept separately and restored after damage or deletion.
Restores take longer than failover, and backups should be tested because an untested backup may fail when needed.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner that compares replication and backup options against a failure scenario practices exactly this reasoning.

lessons.plain: When a service is running, the team needs a small set of readings to know whether users are happy and whether trouble is coming. Many engineering teams, including Google's own practice, boil this down to four signals. Latency is how long a request takes to finish. Traffic is how much demand arrives, such as requests per second. Saturation is how full the most squeezed resource is, such as processor time, memory, or a line of waiting work. Errors are the share of requests that fail. Think of a car dashboard: speed, fuel use, engine heat, and warning lights each tell you something different, and together they tell you whether the trip is going well.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop's checkout page starts taking eight seconds to load during a sale. Server processors are at 99% busy, yet few customers see an error page. Which of the four signals does the processor reading describe, and which signal would show whether customers are actually failing?
lessons.teach:
Latency is the time a request takes from start to finish, measured as the user experiences it, and it should be tracked for successful requests separately from failed ones, because a fast error page can hide a problem. Traffic is the demand on the system, usually counted as requests per second or active sessions. Saturation is how full the most constrained resource is: processor time, memory, disk, network bandwidth, or the length of a queue of waiting work. A system near full saturation has little room to absorb a spike. Errors are the rate of requests that fail, either explicitly (such as an HTTP 500 response) or implicitly (a reply that is wrong or too slow to be useful).

Why these four work together: traffic explains why load changed, saturation says how close the system is to its limit, and latency and errors show what users actually feel. Any one alone can mislead. High processor use with no errors may be fine; rising errors with low processor use may point to a slow database behind the service.

Worked example: a vehicle-tracking API. At 09:00, traffic rises from 200 to 800 requests per second. Saturation climbs from 40% to 98% of processor capacity. Because requests now wait in a queue, the 95th-percentile latency (the time within which 95 of every 100 requests finish) jumps from 120 ms to 2.4 s. Some requests then time out, and the error rate rises from 0.1% to 6%. Each signal moved for a reason the others explain.

Common mistake: reporting only the average latency. An average of 150 ms can hide that one request in twenty takes many seconds, which is exactly what frustrated users notice. Use percentiles instead.

Consequence: when saturation reaches its ceiling, queues grow, latency rises first, and then timeouts turn into errors. Watching saturation and latency gives early warning before errors appear.

The four signals give a team an early, shared picture of whether a service is healthy, and they show where to look next.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery company runs an order API. During a lunchtime promotion, the team records these facts. Traffic rose from 50 to 220 requests per second. The database connection pool, which is the fixed set of database connections the service shares, reached 99% in use, so it is the most constrained resource. The 95th-percentile latency (the time within which 95 of every 100 requests finish) rose from 300 ms to 6 s. Step 4, which you must complete: in a sample of 1,000 requests, 30 returned HTTP 500 errors, and 200 returned 200 OK but after more than 5 s, which the team treats as too slow to be useful. Using the teaching definition that a too-slow reply counts as an error, what is the error rate for this sample?
choices: 20%, because only the too-slow replies count and the 30 explicit errors are ignored
23%, because 230 of the 1,000 requests failed either explicitly or implicitly
3%, because only the explicit HTTP 500 replies count as errors
0.23%, because the sample size should be divided by 100 before counting
questions.why: Errors include both explicit failures and implicit ones such as replies too slow to be useful, so 30 plus 200 gives 230 out of 1,000, which is 23%.

questions.prompt: A streaming service's team wants to know how close its video API is to its limit before users start to notice trouble. Which of the four signals most directly answers how full the most constrained resource is?
choices: Latency, because it measures how long each request takes
Saturation, because it shows how full the most constrained resource, such as processor time or a waiting queue, is
Errors, because they count failed requests
Traffic, because it counts requests per second
questions.why: Saturation is defined as how full the most constrained resource is, which is the signal that shows how close the system is to its limit, while traffic only shows demand and errors show failures that have already happened.

questions.prompt: A music app reports a mean (average) response time of 90 ms for its catalogue API. However, about 1 in 25 requests takes around 4 s. A manager says the service is healthy because the average is low. What is the best correction?
choices: Keep the average, since a low mean proves that no user sees a slow reply
Report only the error rate, since latency does not matter when requests succeed
Remove the slow requests from the data so the average looks accurate
Report the 95th-percentile latency for successful requests, since a low average can hide the slow tail that users notice
questions.why: The teaching text says an average can hide that a small share of requests is very slow, so percentiles and separate tracking of successful requests show what users actually experience.

questions.prompt: A reporting dashboard runs on a service whose processor use stays around 30% all day. Over the same period, its error rate climbs from 0.1% to 3%. Which conclusion best follows from the four signals?
choices: Traffic must have fallen, which explains the errors
The processor is the bottleneck, so the team should buy larger machines
The errors are not real, because the processor is far from full
Low processor use with rising errors may point to a slow component behind the service, such as a database, so the team should look there next
questions.why: The four signals explain each other, and rising errors with low processor use suggests a slow dependency behind the service, which is the place to investigate next.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only ever watched a single server's CPU graph why latency, traffic, saturation and errors are read together, and name one limit of these signals or one tradeoff in choosing what to alert on.
lessons.modelAnswer: A CPU graph tells you one thing about one resource, but users don't experience CPU. Latency and errors describe what users feel: slow answers and failed answers. Traffic tells you how much demand is arriving, so you can tell whether a change in the other signals came from more work or from a fault. Saturation tells you how close the most constrained part is to its limit, which is what lets you act before errors start. The main limit is that these signals are only as good as their labels: a fast error page looks healthy on latency alone, so you split latency by success or failure. The tradeoff is timing. Alerting on saturation early gives you time to react but can create noise when a spike passes by itself, while alerting only on errors is less noisy but means users already see the problem. Set thresholds that leave room to respond.
rubricPoints: Names all four signals and defines each in one plain sentence.
Explains that the signals work together, with traffic as the cause and latency and errors as the user-facing result.
Gives a limit, such as averages hiding slow requests or a fast error looking healthy.
Describes the tradeoff of alerting early on saturation versus late on errors.

suggested.rationale: That incident is about capacity running out during a traffic surge, which is where traffic, saturation, latency and errors get read together.

lessons.plain: When a team runs a service that other people depend on, it needs a shared way to talk about whether that service is working well. Three terms cover it. A service level indicator is a measurement, such as the share of requests that succeed or how long they take. A service level objective is the target you aim for on that measurement, such as 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over a month. A service level agreement is a promise made to a customer, usually with a consequence such as credits or a refund if it is missed. Think of the indicator as a speedometer, the objective as the speed you aim to hold, and the agreement as a speed limit written into a contract.
lessons.guessPrompt: A streaming app team says their service is reliable. Before reading on, what would you need to measure to check that claim, and how would you decide whether the result is good enough?
lessons.teach:
A service level indicator (SLI) is a measurement of one aspect of how a service behaves, usually written as a ratio between 0 and 1 or as a percentage, such as good requests divided by all requests. How fast responses arrive and how fresh the data is can also be indicators. A good indicator reflects what users actually experience.

A service level objective (SLO) is the target an SLI should meet over a stated time window, such as 99.9 percent of requests succeeding across 30 days. The team sets it internally to guide engineering decisions.

A service level agreement (SLA) is a formal promise to customers. It is usually looser than the internal SLO so there is a margin for error, and it normally carries a remedy such as service credits if it is missed.

Worked example: an order API handles 1,000,000 requests in a month and 999,200 succeed. The SLI is 999,200 divided by 1,000,000, or 99.92 percent. The SLO is 99.9 percent, so the team is inside its objective. The SLA promised 99.5 percent, so no credits are owed.

Common mistake: setting an SLO of 100 percent. Nothing achieves that without unlimited spending, and it leaves no room for maintenance or change. A related mistake is writing an SLA tighter than the SLO, which leaves no margin before a contract breach.

In a running system, an SLO implies an error budget. At 99.9 percent, 0.1 percent of requests may fail. When that budget is spent, teams often slow releases and focus on reliability work.

SLIs measure, SLOs target, and SLAs promise.

questions.prompt: A file-upload service at a different company handles 2,400,000 requests in one week, and 2,377,200 of them succeed. Its internal SLO is 99.5 percent over that same week. Step 1 is done: the SLI is 2,377,200 divided by 2,400,000, which is 99.05 percent. Step 2 is done: the allowed failures are 0.5 percent of 2,400,000, which is 12,000. Step 3 is the one missing: work out how many failures actually happened, what share of the allowed budget that uses, and whether the budget is overspent.
choices: 22,800 failures, which is 190 percent of the budget, so it is overspent by 10,800
22,800 failures, so the SLA is breached but the SLO still holds
10,800 failures, leaving 90 percent of the budget unused
The budget is not overspent, because 99.05 percent is above 99 percent
questions.why: Failures are 2,400,000 minus 2,377,200, which is 22,800; against an allowance of 12,000 that is 190 percent, so the error budget is overspent by 10,800.

questions.prompt: A checkout service counts the requests that return a valid response within 300 milliseconds, divided by all checkout requests. What is that ratio?
choices: A service level agreement, because it is a promise to customers
A service level indicator, because it measures one aspect of how the service behaves
A service level objective, because it is a target the team sets
An error budget, because it counts the requests that were allowed to fail
questions.why: A ratio of good events to all events that measures how the service behaves is an SLI; the target is the SLO and the customer promise is the SLA.

questions.prompt: A storage team sets its internal objective at 100 percent of requests succeeding over a month. Which problem follows directly from that choice?
choices: The error budget becomes larger, so the team can release more often
Every request counts as good, so the team no longer needs an indicator
Nothing achieves that without unlimited spending, and no room is left for maintenance or change
The objective turns into a service level agreement automatically, because customers can see it
questions.why: A 100 percent target cannot be reached cheaply and leaves no allowance for failures, which is why the course treats it as a common mistake.

questions.prompt: A ticketing platform's internal SLO is 99.5 percent over a month, and its customer contract (the SLA) promises 99.9 percent for the same month with service credits if missed. What is the main risk of this arrangement?
choices: The SLO protects the team, so credits are never owed
Customers can be owed credits while the internal SLO still reads as met, leaving no margin before breach
Nothing, since the SLO always governs what customers are owed
The error budget grows, because a stricter SLA gives the team more room
questions.why: An SLA tighter than the SLO removes the margin that the SLA should have, so a contract breach can occur while the internal target still looks fine.

lessons.explainPrompt: A product manager wants to promise customers 99.99 percent availability in the contract. Explain to a teammate what the SLI, SLO and SLA would each be in this case, and name one limit or tradeoff of promising that number.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would explain it as three layers. The SLI is what we measure, for example the share of checkout requests that return a successful response, counted every minute. The SLO is our internal target on that measurement, perhaps 99.95 percent over 30 days, set tighter than the contract so we get warning before we breach. The SLA is the contractual promise, here 99.99 percent, with service credits if we miss it. The tradeoff is that 99.99 percent allows only about four minutes of downtime per month, so every planned change and every dependency outage uses up that allowance. Before we sign, we need to check that our architecture, redundancy and change process can actually hit that number, because the promise is expensive to keep and the penalty is real.
rubricPoints: An SLI is a measured indicator that reflects what users experience.
An SLO is an internal target for an SLI over a stated time window.
An SLA is an external contractual promise, usually looser than the SLO, with a remedy if missed.
A very high target leaves little error budget, so it is costly to achieve and easy to breach.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the three layers and their tradeoff back to a teammate is the core skill for this vocabulary objective.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Parcel's Cloud Memo
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Parcel Co. is a fictional regional courier that runs its own servers in a back room at its Columbus depot. Its operations director, Nia, has sent the board a memo that says: 'Moving to cloud will make us faster, cheaper, and global.' Cloud means renting computing resources over a network from a provider instead of owning the machines yourself. Digital transformation means changing how a business works and serves customers using digital tools, which is more than swapping hardware. Infrastructure means the underlying servers, storage, and networks that software runs on. Brightwater's team is also weighing a split plan: keep the depot's barcode-scanning system on its own servers (on-premises, meaning physically in or near the business), while moving the customer tracking website and billing system to Google Cloud. Latency means the delay between sending a request and receiving the reply, usually measured in milliseconds. Use the memo and plan to answer the tasks below. 1. Separate the three terms cloud, digital transformation, and infrastructure as they are used in Nia's memo, and say which of them the word 'faster' really points to. 2. Take the claim 'cloud gives us global reach.' Say specifically what would change for Brightwater's customers, and name the Google Cloud differentiator that supports it, if any applies. 3. For the split plan, name the architecture (private, hybrid, or multicloud), give one business benefit and one risk, and explain why scanner latency argues for keeping the scanning system local.
subParts: Separate cloud, digital transformation, and infrastructure in the memo, and identify what 'faster' refers to
Say what changes for customers under 'global reach' and name the supporting Google Cloud differentiator
Name the architecture of the split plan, give one benefit and one risk, and explain the latency argument for keeping scanning local
modelAnswer: Cloud is renting computing resources over a network from a provider. Digital transformation is the broader change in how the business operates and serves customers using digital tools, so cloud is one enabler of it, not the same thing. Infrastructure is the servers, storage, and networks underneath the software. The memo's 'faster' points mainly to digital transformation outcomes such as agility (how quickly the business can change and ship new features or processes) and speed of delivery, which cloud infrastructure makes possible. Common mistake: treating the three as interchangeable, so the board believes that moving servers alone equals transformation. Consequence: if only the servers move and the old approval processes stay, the business is not actually faster.

Global reach means customers in distant places can use Brightwater's services with less delay and more reliability. For example, a customer in Denver opens the tracking page. The request enters Google's network at the edge location nearest to Denver (a point of presence close to users), then travels over Google's private network to the region hosting the tracking application (a geographic area containing several isolated zones). The response returns the same way. The supporting differentiator is Google's global network, which carries traffic over Google-owned fiber rather than the public internet for much of the route. Common mistake: assuming global reach means data is automatically stored everywhere. Brightwater must still choose which regions hold its data, since placement affects latency and data residency rules. Consequence: hosting the app in one distant region adds delay for nearby customers even though the network is global.

The split plan is a hybrid cloud, meaning a mix of on-premises systems and public cloud services that work together. A business benefit is that the scanners keep running locally, and the website and billing can scale up during peak shipping weeks without buying servers. A risk is that two environments must be secured, patched, and kept in sync, which adds complexity. Scanner latency argues for local hosting because each barcode scan needs a fast confirmation. If each scan waits for a round trip to a distant cloud region, the delay adds up across hundreds of scans a minute, and an internet outage would stop scanning entirely. A local system answers in a few milliseconds and keeps working when the connection drops. Common mistake: assuming hybrid automatically lowers cost; duplicate environments can raise it. Consequence: without budgeting for both sides, the company pays for two systems without saving money.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lane Outfitters: Choosing the Right Data Home
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lane Outfitters is a fictional online retailer of hiking and camping gear with about 40 employees. It runs a small store website, a warehouse with scanned paperwork, and a growing set of reports that its managers want to read each morning. The company is moving its data to Google Cloud and has asked you, the new engineer, to recommend a product for each need. Keep in mind that a product that could hold the data is not automatically the product that fits the job. Terms used here: a relational database stores information in tables of rows and columns linked by shared key values, and it is designed for many small reads and writes that must stay accurate together. A data warehouse stores large amounts of history in a form built for analysis questions that scan many rows at once. Object storage keeps whole files, such as images or PDFs, as objects in a flat container with a unique name each. Streaming means events are sent and processed continuously as they happen rather than in a nightly batch. The company has four needs. First, the website's order system must record each purchase and stock change accurately, with a standard SQL interface, and the data fits comfortably in one region. Second, managers want monthly sales trends and dashboards built from years of order history. Third, a box of seven-year-old scanned invoices must be kept for legal reasons and is almost never opened. Fourth, the website produces a constant stream of click events that the marketing team wants to see on a live chart within seconds. For each need, name the Google Cloud product you would recommend and explain why it fits, and describe one mistake you would avoid. Sub-tasks: 1. Recommend a product for the order system and explain why. 2. Recommend the product and dashboard tool for the managers' trend reports and explain why. 3. Recommend a Cloud Storage class for the invoice archive and explain the cost trade-off. 4. Describe the products that would carry and process the click stream to the live chart, and explain what each one does.
subParts: Recommend a product for the order system and explain why.
Recommend the product and dashboard tool for the managers' trend reports and explain why.
Recommend a Cloud Storage class for the invoice archive and explain the cost trade-off.
Describe the products that would carry and process the click stream to the live chart, and explain what each one does.
modelAnswer: Cloud SQL is a fully managed relational database service: Google runs the server, backups, and patching, while you keep a standard SQL interface (the common language for querying tables). It fits the order system because purchases and stock changes need to be recorded accurately together, which is what relational databases are built for, and the data volume is modest and in one region. A common mistake is choosing BigQuery for this job because it also holds tables; BigQuery is built for analysis scans, not for many small, accurate writes from a live website. Consequence: putting transactions in an analytics warehouse can make order updates slow or inconsistent during busy sales.

BigQuery is Google Cloud's serverless data warehouse, meaning you do not manage servers and it can scan very large tables to answer analysis questions such as monthly trends. Looker is the business intelligence tool that connects to BigQuery and turns those results into reports and dashboards that managers can read and share. Together they fit a need for historical trends across years of orders. A common mistake is pointing the managers' dashboards straight at the live order database, which adds analysis load to the system that takes customer purchases. Consequence: the website can slow down during the morning report run.

Cloud Storage is object storage, and its classes are priced by how often you expect to read the data. Standard is for frequent access, Nearline and Coldline are for less frequent access with lower storage prices but retrieval fees, and Archive is the lowest storage price for data you rarely touch, with the highest retrieval cost and minimum storage period. Autoclass can move objects between classes automatically based on how they are used. For seven-year-old invoices that are almost never opened but must be kept, Archive gives the lowest monthly cost. A common mistake is choosing Archive for files the team reads every week, which makes frequent access expensive. Consequence: a surprise bill from retrieval fees and early deletion charges.

Pub/Sub is a managed messaging service that receives events from many sources and holds them so that other systems can read them as they arrive, which decouples the website from downstream processing. Dataflow is a managed stream and batch processing service that takes those events, transforms them (for example counting clicks per minute), and writes the results to a destination such as BigQuery or a live dashboard. Together they form a streaming pipeline that gives marketing near real-time insight rather than a next-day report. A common mistake is sending click events directly from the website into the analysis database one by one, which can overload it during traffic spikes. Consequence: lost or delayed events and a chart that lags behind reality.

scenarios.title: Harbor Peak Outfitters: Photo Tags, Return Predictions and Messy Data
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Peak Outfitters is a fictional online retailer of camping and hiking gear with about 40 staff. Its operations lead, Dana, is new to cloud and has three requests. First, the merchandising team wants every product photo tagged with labels such as tent, stove or backpack, without training anything in-house. Second, the team wants to estimate which orders are likely to be returned in the next 60 days, using three years of order history that already sits in BigQuery, the company's data warehouse (a large store built for analysing tables of data), and they do not want to copy that data into another tool. Third, before anyone trusts either result, the data analyst notices that the customer table has duplicate rows, some postcodes are blank, and order dates appear in two different formats. Answer the following.

1. Name the Google Cloud product that best fits the photo-tagging request, say whether it is pre-trained or custom, and explain the trade-off between speed and effort.

2. Explain what BigQuery ML is and describe how the team could build a return-prediction model using standard SQL without moving the data.

3. Name the data quality dimensions the customer table violates, match each problem to one dimension, and explain why this must be fixed before the choice of model matters.
subParts: Photo tagging product choice
BigQuery ML return model
Data quality dimensions
modelAnswer: The best fit is the Vision API. It is a pre-trained image analysis service, meaning Google has already trained a model on very large collections of images, so Harbor Peak can send a photo and receive labels, each with a confidence score (how sure the model is), without building a model of its own. This is the fastest option and needs little machine learning expertise. The trade-off is that the labels are generic and may not separate Harbor Peak's own product variants, such as two similar tent models. If that precision matters, the company would need a custom model, for example one built with AutoML on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform using its own labelled photos. That gives more differentiation (a result competitors cannot easily copy) but takes longer and needs more effort and skill. For a first pass, pre-trained is the faster, lower-effort choice.

BigQuery ML is a feature that lets you create and run machine learning models inside BigQuery itself, using standard SQL (the common language for asking questions of database tables). Because the model trains where the data already lives, nothing has to be exported. In practice, the team would write a CREATE MODEL statement that names a model type and points to a query selecting the inputs, called features, such as order value, product category and days since purchase, plus a label column that records whether each past order was returned. Once trained, a prediction query using ML.PREDICT scores new orders. A common mistake is including a column that only exists after the outcome is known, such as a refund date. The model then looks highly accurate in testing but fails on real new orders, which would lead Harbor Peak to stock the wrong amounts of stock based on a false sense of reliability.

Duplicate rows violate uniqueness, because the same customer or order appears more than once, which double counts returns and distorts every average. Blank postcodes violate completeness, because required values are missing. Dates appearing in two formats violate consistency, because the same kind of information is stored in different ways across records; it could also be seen as a validity problem if one format is not allowed at all. Accuracy and timeliness would need separate checks against real-world records and recent update times. These problems must be fixed first because a model learns whatever patterns the data contains. Duplicates and mixed date formats can make a model find patterns that do not exist, so a more advanced algorithm will not rescue it. Data quality is a prerequisite for a working model, not an optional clean-up step, and skipping it can lead to wrong forecasts that drive real purchasing decisions.

scenarios.title: Brindle Peak Outfitters: Choosing a Modernization Path
scenarios.scenario: Brindle Peak Outfitters is a fictional online outdoor-gear retailer with about 120 employees. Its engineering team runs three workloads in its own data center, and leadership has asked you, a newly hired cloud engineer, to recommend a path for each. A workload means any application or job together with the servers and data it depends on. Before recommending anything, the team completed discovery and assessment, meaning they inventoried every workload and rated each one by how much business value it has, how often it is used, and how hard it is to move. The three workloads are: (A) a legacy returns-report tool written 12 years ago that two staff members run once a month and that nobody has changed since; (B) an image-resizing service that turns product photos into thumbnails, which receives almost no traffic most days but spikes to thousands of requests during flash sales, and whose code is already packaged in containers; and (C) a product catalog API that the company wants to offer, for a fee, to three retail partners who would build their own storefronts on it. Write your recommendation for each workload. Tasks: 1. For workload A, name the migration approach you would choose from the options retire, retain, rehost, replatform, refactor and reimagine, and explain why rehosting is the near-miss you would reject. 2. For workload B, choose between Cloud Run and Compute Engine virtual machines, say whether Spot VMs would suit it, and explain why. 3. For workload C, say whether the company should expose the catalog API directly or manage it with Apigee, and explain what Apigee adds for paid partner access.
subParts: Workload A: migration approach and why rehost is the near miss
Workload B: Cloud Run versus Compute Engine, and Spot VMs
Workload C: exposing the API directly versus Apigee for paid partners
modelAnswer: Recommend retire, or at minimum retain until the two staff confirm they still need it. Retire means switching a workload off on purpose because it no longer delivers enough value. Retain means keeping it where it is for now and revisiting later. Since the tool runs once a month, has no owner and has not changed in 12 years, the first step is to ask whether a replacement report or a simple spreadsheet export would cover the need. If the two staff still need the output, a sensible interim choice is to rehost it, which means moving the same software onto a virtual machine in the cloud with little or no code change. Rehosting is the near miss: it is quick, but it moves an unloved workload into a new home and keeps paying for a virtual machine that sits idle 29 days a month. A replatform or refactor would only make sense if the tool were used heavily. Consequence: moving a dead tool costs money every month without adding value.

Recommend Cloud Run. Cloud Run is a serverless compute service, meaning Google runs the servers and you supply a container, which is a packaged bundle of an application and everything it needs to run. Cloud Run scales to zero when no requests arrive and adds instances during spikes, so Brindle Peak pays for the sales-day load rather than for idle capacity the rest of the month. Compute Engine virtual machines would work, but you would manage operating systems, scaling rules and load balancing yourself, and you would pay for machines that sit mostly idle. Spot VMs are discounted virtual machines that Google can reclaim with very short notice. They suit fault-tolerant batch jobs that can restart safely; for a service answering live customer web requests, an interruption during a sale would show up as failed thumbnails, so Spot VMs are a poor fit here, although they could suit a nightly bulk re-resize job. Common mistake: choosing Spot VMs only for their lower price without asking whether the job can tolerate being stopped mid-task.

Recommend Apigee. An API is an application programming interface, a defined way for one piece of software to request data or actions from another. Exposing the catalog API directly means partners call the company's servers straight away, with no control over who calls, how often, or how usage is billed. Apigee is Google's API management product: it sits in front of the API as a gateway that handles authentication of partner keys, enforces usage quotas, publishes a developer portal with documentation, collects usage analytics, and can meter calls so the company can charge partners by volume. Because the business goal is paid access, the metering and per-partner controls are the deciding factor. Common mistake: assuming an API can be monetized simply by putting a price list on a web page; without metering and key management, the company cannot prove or bill usage. Consequence: without a gateway, one partner's traffic spike can slow the catalog for everyone, including the company's own storefront.

scenarios.title: Kestrel Ledger's Bad Week in the Cloud
scenarios.scenario: Kestrel Ledger Co. is a fictional firm of 120 staff that makes invoicing software for small shops. It is moving its customer billing app and file storage to Google Cloud. Three things went wrong in one week. First, a finance clerk received a phishing email, which is a fake message designed to trick a person into typing a password on a lookalike login page. She typed her password, and an attacker tried to sign in with it, but Kestrel had not turned on a second login step. Second, a developer made a Cloud Storage bucket, which is a container for stored files, readable by anyone on the internet, so a folder of customer invoices was publicly visible for two days. Third, a contractor from an outside firm still held full administrator rights on the billing project. The security lead must answer the following. 1. Name the threat in the phishing event, and say whether turning on two-step verification for the clerk's login is Google's job or Kestrel's, and why. 2. Name the problem with the public bucket, say whether it is a Google or customer responsibility, and explain which encryption usage state (in transit or at rest) protects the invoices in each situation. 3. Explain the difference between authentication, authorization, and auditing using the contractor's account, and recommend the least privilege change you would make.
subParts: Phishing threat and who owns two-step verification
Public bucket, responsibility, and encryption states
Authentication, authorization, and auditing for the contractor
modelAnswer: The threat is phishing, a social-engineering attack in which a fake message tricks a person into revealing credentials. Two-step verification, also called multi-factor authentication (MFA), asks for a second proof of identity, such as a phone prompt, in addition to the password. Turning it on and requiring it for accounts is Kestrel's responsibility. Google supplies the feature and can help enforce it, but the customer decides who must use it and configures it on its own accounts. Worked example: the attacker had the clerk's password but not her phone, so the second step blocks the sign-in. Common mistake: assuming a secure cloud provider prevents phishing. The people and account settings are the customer's to manage. Consequence: without a second factor, a stolen password alone gives access to customer invoices.

The problem is a misconfiguration: the bucket's access settings allowed public reading. Google secures the storage service itself, but whoever sets the access controls decides who can read the files, so this is the customer's responsibility. Encryption in transit protects data while it moves between a user and Google's services, typically using TLS (Transport Layer Security, the protocol that encrypts network connections); this protects the invoices when they are downloaded over the internet. Encryption at rest protects data stored on disks; Google encrypts stored data by default. Common mistake: believing encryption at rest keeps the public out. The service decrypts transparently for any identity that the access settings allow, so a public bucket is readable even though it is encrypted. Consequence: customer invoices were exposed, creating a data breach with business and legal impact. The fix is to block public access and grant read access only to named users or groups.

Authentication is proving who you are, such as a password plus a second factor. Authorization is deciding what that verified identity may do, managed through IAM (Identity and Access Management, the system that assigns roles and permissions). Auditing is recording and reviewing what was done, using logs such as Cloud Logging audit logs. In the contractor's case, signing in shows authentication worked, but the full administrator role is authorization far beyond what a billing task needs. Least privilege means granting only the permissions required for the task and only for as long as needed. Recommendation: replace the administrator role with a narrow role such as read-only access to the billing data, set an end date on the contractor's access, and review the audit logs for activity during the contract. Common mistake: treating a successful login as proof that access is safe. Consequence: a compromised contractor account with full administrator rights could delete or expose the whole billing environment.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Parcel's doubled cloud bill and slow tracking pages
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Parcel Co. is a fictional mid-sized company that runs an online parcel-tracking website. Until last year its servers sat in a rented room in its own office, bought up front as capital expenditure (CapEx, money spent once on long-lived assets such as servers). It has now moved to Google Cloud, where it pays for resources as it uses them, which is operating expenditure (OpEx, recurring day-to-day spending). Three problems have appeared this quarter. First, the monthly invoice is double what finance expected, and nobody in engineering is clear on who may approve new spending. Second, customers say tracking pages load slowly on busy afternoons, and the team has no shared way to say how fast is fast enough. Third, a nightly job that rebuilds delivery reports could run on cheaper machines, but the team is unsure whether that is safe. You are the new cloud operations lead. Answer the following.

1. Explain how the move from CapEx to OpEx changes the way Brightwater should measure total cost of ownership (TCO, the full cost of running something over its life, including staff time, power and idle capacity, not just the sticker price). Then name one Google Cloud control that helps finance see and limit spending each month.

2. Brightwater's projects sit in a resource hierarchy (the nested structure of organization, folders, projects and resources that Google Cloud uses to group things). Say at which level budget and access decisions should be made, and explain what inheritance (a rule set at a higher level automatically applying to everything below it) buys the company.

3. For the slow pages, name the four signals used to measure system health (latency, traffic, saturation, errors). Then propose one service level indicator (SLI, a measured number describing service quality) and one service level objective (SLO, the internal target for that number).

4. For the nightly job, decide whether Spot VMs (discounted virtual machines that Google Cloud can reclaim at short notice) or Dynamic Workload Scheduler (a service that queues and times batch work so it starts when capacity is available) fits better, and state what the team must accept in return.
subParts: TCO shift from CapEx to OpEx and one spending-control tool
Budget and access decisions placed in the resource hierarchy, and inheritance
The four signals, plus one SLI and one SLO for page speed
Choosing Spot VMs or Dynamic Workload Scheduler for the nightly job and its trade-off
modelAnswer: Under CapEx the company paid once and spread the cost over years, but under OpEx the cost arrives monthly and rises or falls with use, so it is easy to overlook. TCO should therefore count staff time, power, maintenance and idle capacity, because a cloud server left running overnight still costs money even when nobody uses it. A useful control is Cloud Billing reports, which break spending down by project, service and label, paired with budget threshold rules that send alerts when spending reaches set percentages of a budget. The common mistake is treating the invoice as something only finance owns; engineering should share ownership of usage, and the consequence of ignoring that is a surprise bill nobody can explain.

Budgets and access should be set at the folder level for policies shared by several teams, and at the project level for one team's own spending. A quota policy (a limit on how much of a resource can be used) or an access role granted on a folder flows down by inheritance to every project below it, so one change applies consistently and supports security, compliance and clearer visibility of which team caused which cost. The mistake to avoid is granting access resource by resource, which becomes hard to manage and leaves gaps; a new project created outside the pattern would then quietly skip the rule.

The four signals are latency (how long requests take), traffic (how much demand arrives), saturation (how full the underlying resources are, such as CPU or connection pools) and errors (how many requests fail). A reasonable SLI is the share of tracking-page requests answered in under 2 seconds, measured at the load balancer over a rolling 30 days. A matching SLO is that 99 percent of those requests meet the 2-second target in each calendar month. The team should set the SLO stricter than any external service level agreement (SLA, the customer-facing promise with consequences). A common mistake is using average response time, which hides the slow tail that customers actually notice.

Spot VMs fit better because the goal is cost, and the nightly report job can tolerate interruption if it is designed for it. The team must accept that Google can reclaim these machines with short notice, so the job should save checkpoints (progress markers) and resume, and it may take longer to finish. Dynamic Workload Scheduler would be the better match if the job needed to wait for guaranteed capacity at a set time. The mistake is running a long job on Spot VMs without checkpointing; a reclaim would then restart the whole job and could miss the morning deadline for delivery reports.
